AI.motivation: Training RL agents on physical robots makes falls costly (damage, no reset), so minimizing falls during training is critical. Existing constrained MDP formulations trade falls off against return, while mixed-policy rollouts with recovery policies introduce bias that importance sampling cannot correct when the recovery policy is deterministic.
AI.method: The core contribution is an unbiased policy-gradient estimator using score function only at safe timesteps, avoiding evaluation of the recovery policy's density. This is supplemented by: (1) a closed-form value for recovery-triggering states when dynamics and recovery are deterministic, and (2) an imitation loss that copies recovery actions only when recovery succeeds.
AI.result: On a three-environment, five-seed benchmark, the algorithm reduces training-time falls by 233x, 48x, and 26x on HalfCheetah, Ant, and Unitree Go1 over standard PPO, matches or exceeds PPO's final reward, and on Ant with unreliable recovery, it is the only method reaching 80% of the best final reward.
AI.conclusion: The proposed drop-in PPO modification effectively minimizes falls during training by removing the bias introduced by recovery policies, achieving dramatic fall reduction while maintaining reward performance, and works where importance sampling fails (deterministic recovery policies).

title: ProofCouncil: An LLM Agent for Solving Open Mathematical Problems
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures. ProofCouncil appears as System A (IMProofBench ProofCouncil) in the official FirstProof second-batch report (arXiv:2606.18119). Code and agent-building library: https://github.com/eth-sri/proof-council
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in solving open problems in mathematics. However, their performance can be further improved through agentic workflows tailored to real-world mathematical practice. To this end, we introduce ProofCouncil, a mathematical agent that is designed to tackle open problems using an author-critic architecture. ProofCouncil served as a submission to the second batch of FirstProof, a challenge consisting of 10 real-world mathematical problems that agents must solve autonomously. Its submissions for 6 of the 10 problems were judged by the referees to be correct up to at most minor revisions, showing the best performance among participating teams. We also evaluate ProofCouncil on 30 open problems collected from mathematical researchers. Among the 21 solutions that received human feedback, 5 were judged completely correct, 2 more were judged promising pending final verification, and a further 8 contained useful partial progress. In this short paper, we describe the development of ProofCouncil and the agent-building library used to create it, which we release as open source to the community.

AI.tldr: ProofCouncil is a mathematical agent using an author-critic architecture that solved 6/10 open problems in the FirstProof challenge (best performance) and achieved 5 completely correct solutions out of 21 evaluated on real mathematical open problems.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise in solving open math problems but can be further improved through agentic workflows tailored to real-world mathematical practice.
AI.method: ProofCouncil uses an author-critic architecture within an agentic workflow, built on a newly released open-source agent-building library.
AI.result: Best performance in FirstProof challenge (6/10 problems correct up to minor revisions); on 30 open problems, 5/21 evaluated solutions were completely correct, 2 more promising, and 8 contained useful partial progress.
AI.conclusion: The author-critic agentic approach significantly improves LLM performance on formal mathematical problem-solving, and the associated library is released as open source.

title: Git-Assistant: Planning-Based Support for Updating Git Repositories
summary: Version control systems are essential for collaborative software development, yet tools like git remain challenging for many practitioners. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for interpreting developer intent, but their effectiveness in repository management tasks is limited by the need for formal reasoning. This work introduces Git-Assistant, an AI-based assistant that combines LLMs with automated planning to support developers in executing non-trivial git operations. The assistant analyzes repository context, translates natural language requests into actionable command sequences, and incorporates planning techniques to ensure correctness and safety. We present a systematic evaluation methodology using synthetic and randomized git environments, comparing the performance of LLM-only and planning-augmented variants across multiple metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating formal reasoning with LLMs improves reliability and reduces errors in repository management, highlighting the potential of hybrid AI approaches for intelligent developer assistance.

AI.tldr: Git-Assistant combines LLMs with automated planning to help developers execute git operations via natural language, showing that planning-augmented variants outperform LLM-only approaches in reliability and error reduction.
AI.motivation: Git and version control systems remain difficult for many practitioners, and while LLMs show promise for interpreting developer intent, they lack formal reasoning capabilities needed for correct and safe repository management.
AI.method: The system integrates LLMs with automated planning techniques: it analyzes repository context, translates natural language requests into actionable command sequences, and incorporates planning for correctness and safety. Evaluation uses synthetic and randomized git environments comparing LLM-only vs. planning-augmented variants.
AI.result: Integrating formal reasoning (automated planning) with LLMs improves reliability and reduces errors in repository management tasks compared to LLM-only approaches.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid AI approaches that combine LLMs with formal reasoning mechanisms are promising for intelligent developer assistance tools, particularly for tasks requiring both natural language understanding and operational correctness.

title: Adaptive Latent Trajectory Anchoring for Action Segmentation Dataset Condensation
summary: Dataset condensation for action segmentation synthesizes compact, informative representations of long, untrimmed video datasets. The existing approach relies on Variational Autoencoders and an iterative latent optimization; it is computationally expensive and suffers from over-smoothed reconstructions and rigid temporal constraints. This paper proposes to shift the condensation paradigm from optimization-based inversion to deterministic latent mapping. By leveraging Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models, we represent action segments as continuous trajectories anchored by sparse latent points in the noise manifold. To maximize representational efficiency, we introduce an adaptive allocation mechanism that dynamically redistributes the anchoring budget based on segment-wise reconstruction difficulty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in segmentation performance across common datasets. Notably, our approach achieves performance parity with real data training while maintaining a condensation ratio of 2.4\% on Breakfast dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper improves dataset condensation for action segmentation by replacing expensive VAE-based iterative optimization with deterministic latent mapping using Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models, achieving state-of-the-art performance with only 2.4% of original data on Breakfast dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing dataset condensation for action segmentation relies on Variational Autoencoders and iterative latent optimization, which is computationally expensive, produces over-smoothed reconstructions, and suffers from rigid temporal constraints.
AI.method: Shifts from optimization-based inversion to deterministic latent mapping using Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models, representing action segments as continuous trajectories anchored by sparse latent points in the noise manifold, with an adaptive allocation mechanism that dynamically redistributes anchoring budget based on segment-wise reconstruction difficulty.
AI.result: Significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across common datasets; achieves performance parity with real data training while maintaining a condensation ratio of 2.4% on Breakfast dataset.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic latent mapping with diffusion models is a more efficient and effective paradigm for action segmentation dataset condensation than optimization-based inversion.

title: BlockServe: Block-Grained Continuous Batching for High-Throughput Diffusion LLM Serving
summary: Efficient serving of diffusion large language models (dLLMs) is hindered by convergence heterogeneity: when batching multiple requests, different sequences converge at different rates, causing faster requests to stall behind slower stragglers and introducing compute bubbles and tail latency. We present BlockServe, a continuous batching framework that integrates block-grained scheduling -- immediately evicting completed requests at block boundaries -- with mixed-state execution that extends dual cache and parallel decoding to heterogeneous batches via gather-scatter indexing. Furthermore, a compute-aware admission controller expands effective batch capacity through token-budgeted refill. On Dream and LLaDA across five benchmarks, BlockServe achieves 1.9--10.6$\times$ throughput over Fast-dLLM with comparable generation quality, establishing block-grained scheduling as a foundation for high-throughput offline dLLM inference.

AI.tldr: BlockServe is a continuous batching framework for diffusion LLMs that uses block-grained scheduling, mixed-state execution with gather-scatter indexing, and compute-aware admission control to address convergence heterogeneity, achieving 1.9-10.6× throughput over Fast-dLLM.
AI.motivation: Efficient serving of diffusion LLMs is hindered by convergence heterogeneity: when batching multiple requests, different sequences converge at different rates, causing faster requests to stall behind slower stragglers, introducing compute bubbles and tail latency.
AI.method: BlockServe integrates block-grained scheduling (evicting completed requests at block boundaries), mixed-state execution extending dual cache and parallel decoding via gather-scatter indexing, and compute-aware admission control using token-budgeted refill.
AI.result: On Dream and LLaDA across five benchmarks, BlockServe achieves 1.9-10.6× throughput over Fast-dLLM with comparable generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Block-grained scheduling establishes a foundation for high-throughput offline dLLM inference.

title: Ceci n'est pas une pipe: AI systems as semantic abstractions
summary: An AI system's output is not the fact or world state it appears to describe, but rather an engineered representation. We propose a semantic framework to describe AI systems, to be able to examine the correctness of such representations. To do so, we distinguish what is justified by accepted domain knowledge, what reference sources say, and what the system can currently use. This allows us to give precise definitions to common failures: extrapolation, refuted or unsupported assertion, sources versus knowledge mismatch, stale or refuted source, added hypotheses, unsupported use... We hope our framework gives a useful vocabulary for specifying and checking AI systems whose outputs, citations, tool calls, and world-changing actions must be justified by reliable claims and explicit authority rather than apparent fluency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a semantic framework for evaluating AI system outputs by distinguishing between justified domain knowledge, reference sources, and system-available information, providing precise definitions for common failure modes like extrapolation, unsupported assertions, and source mismatches.
AI.motivation: AI system outputs are engineered representations, not facts or world states, yet they are often treated as authoritative. There is a need for a rigorous framework to examine the correctness of such representations.
AI.method: The authors develop a semantic framework that distinguishes three categories: (1) what is justified by accepted domain knowledge, (2) what reference sources say, and (3) what the system can currently use. They then provide precise formal definitions for various failure modes.
AI.result: The framework yields precise definitions for common AI system failures including extrapolation, refuted assertions, unsupported assertions, sources-versus-knowledge mismatch, stale/refuted sources, added hypotheses, and unsupported use.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a useful vocabulary for specifying and checking AI systems whose outputs, citations, tool calls, and actions must be justified by reliable claims and explicit authority rather than apparent fluency.

title: How Far Are We from Detecting Flaky Tests? On the Limits of Code-Based Detection
summary: Flaky tests pass and fail on the same code version, weakening the signal of test results and disrupting continuous integration (CI) pipelines. Code-based flakiness detectors report strong benchmark results, yet their use in practice remains limited. We argue that the field is studying the wrong problem: Flakiness is not a static property of test code, which often lacks the information needed to decide whether a test is flaky. Analyzing three code-based detectors operating on test code, we found that widely used benchmarks contain shortcuts that inflate reported F1 scores and that evaluation protocols overstate generalizability. To control for these shortcuts, we curated two datasets. The first, C-IDoFT (54,468 unit tests from 57 GitHub projects), keeps a developer-confirmed subset of IDoFT's flaky tests and rebuilds only the non-flaky class from repeated executions instead of fixed versions of flaky tests. C-IDoFT is a controlled counterfactual, not a benchmark for reuse. Our CodeBERT reimplementations of two published detectors scored far above its constant baselines under the published cross-validation protocol but no better than them once projects were separated. The high scores rested on the labeling shortcut and the evaluation protocol, not on the test code. On FlakeBench, a benchmark restricted to flakiness types typically recognizable from test code, and the same project-disjoint protocol, the models identified nearly all flaky tests. The second dataset, mined from CI logs, contains 86 flaky end-to-end tests that passed and failed on the same commit. The test code and CI log yielded a cause for 42% of them; the other 58% required further execution evidence. Rather than abandoning flakiness prediction, we reframe it around whether an observed failure is flaky and how likely a test is to fail given its execution environment. Our datasets and CI-mining method support this direction.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that code-based flaky test detectors address the wrong problem, as flakiness is not a static property of test code. It shows that published benchmarks contain shortcuts inflating F1 scores and evaluation protocols overstate generalizability. Using controlled datasets (C-IDoFT and CI-mined logs), the authors demonstrate that detectors perform no better than constant baselines on project-disjoint protocols. They reframe flakiness prediction around observed failure flakiness and execution environment likelihood.
AI.motivation: Code-based flaky test detectors report strong benchmark results but are rarely adopted in practice. The authors hypothesize this gap exists because flakiness is not a static property of test code—it depends on execution environment and timing. The field has been studying the wrong problem by treating flakiness as determinable from test code alone.
AI.method: Analyzed three code-based flaky test detectors and identified shortcuts in widely used benchmarks (e.g., IDoFT) that inflate reported F1 scores. Created two controlled datasets: (1) C-IDoFT, a counterfactual dataset with developer-confirmed flaky tests and rebuilt non-flaky classes, and (2) a CI-mined dataset of 86 flaky end-to-end tests from CI logs. Reimplemented two published detectors using CodeBERT and evaluated under cross-validation vs. project-disjoint protocols.
AI.result: Under cross-validation, CodeBERT reimplementations scored far above constant baselines, but under project-disjoint protocols they performed no better than constant baselines on C-IDoFT. On FlakeBench (restricted to flakiness types recognizable from test code), models identified nearly all flaky tests. In the CI-mined dataset, test code + CI log explained only 42% of flaky tests; 58% required further execution evidence.
AI.conclusion: Flakiness prediction should be reframed around whether an observed failure is flaky and how likely a test is to fail given its execution environment, rather than predicting flakiness from static test code alone.

title: REBASE: Reference-Background Subspace Elimination for Training-Free In-Context Segmentation
summary: Training-free in-context segmentation enables new object categories to be introduced at inference time from a single annotated reference image, eliminating the retraining and memory overhead of class-incremental learning. Recent approaches achieve this by combining vision foundation models for semantic correspondence with promptable segmentation networks like SAM. However, their performance is fundamentally limited by the quality of the cross-image similarity map; shared contextual backgrounds between the reference and query systematically elevate similarity in non-target regions, degrading prompt localization. We present REBASE, a training-free framework that explicitly suppresses these spurious contextual correspondences. Our method identifies the low-rank background feature subspace from the reference image and project the reference and query features onto its orthogonal complement in closed form, yielding cleaner semantic matching. We then generate positive point prompts using similarity-weighted farthest-point sampling, paired with a refined dense similarity prior. Without any training or parameter updates, our approach establishes a new state of the art among training-free methods on PACO-Part, FSS-1000, and cross-domain datasets such as ISIC2018, demonstrating that explicit background subspace removal is a highly effective principle for one-shot localization.

AI.tldr: REBASE is a training-free in-context segmentation method that suppresses spurious background correspondences by projecting features onto the orthogonal complement of a low-rank background subspace identified from the reference image, achieving SOTA among training-free methods on PACO-Part, FSS-1000, and cross-domain datasets like ISIC2018.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free in-context segmentation methods are fundamentally limited by the quality of cross-image similarity maps, where shared contextual backgrounds between reference and query images systematically elevate similarity in non-target regions, degrading prompt localization for segmentation models like SAM.
AI.method: REBASE identifies a low-rank background feature subspace from the reference image, then projects both reference and query features onto its orthogonal complement in closed form to suppress spurious contextual correspondences. It generates positive point prompts using similarity-weighted farthest-point sampling paired with a refined dense similarity prior.
AI.result: Without any training or parameter updates, REBASE establishes a new state of the art among training-free methods on PACO-Part, FSS-1000, and cross-domain datasets such as ISIC2018.
AI.conclusion: Explicit background subspace removal is a highly effective principle for one-shot localization, demonstrating that cleaner semantic matching can be achieved without retraining or parameter updates.

title: TSRouter: Dynamic Modality-Model Selection for Time Series Reasoning
summary: Time series reasoning is essential for real-world problem-solving. While both Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can reason about time-series data, their capabilities are complementary: LLMs process time series as text sequences and thus preserve exact numerical understanding, but struggle with global patterns, whereas VLMs efficiently capture these patterns by visualizing time series but may lose fine-grained details. Moreover, models vary significantly in task-specific expertise and inference costs. Dynamically selecting the most suitable modality and model for each query is therefore crucial, yet challenging because it requires modeling the complex interactions among tasks, queries, modalities, and models, which carry rich contextual signals. To this end, we introduce TSRouter, a graph-based dynamic routing framework. TSRouter constructs a heterogeneous graph of task, query, modality, and model nodes to contextualize the interactions among query characteristics, modality attributes, and model capabilities. TSRouter formulates routing as a candidate scoring problem, where each modality-model pair is evaluated based on user-defined performance-cost preferences to select the optimal candidate. Comprehensive evaluations on 4 distinct time series reasoning tasks reveal that TSRouter substantially outperforms diverse baselines with 16\% to 46\% relative improvements. Furthermore, TSRouter demonstrates robust zero-shot plug-and-play generalization to unseen models and novel tasks and preserves high performance while reducing computational overhead through cost-aware optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/tianyi-lab/TSRouter.

AI.tldr: TSRouter is a graph-based dynamic routing framework that selects the optimal modality-model combination (LLM or VLM) for time series reasoning tasks by modeling interactions among tasks, queries, modalities, and models via a heterogeneous graph, achieving 16-46% relative improvements and zero-shot generalization to unseen models/tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs and VLMs have complementary strengths (exact numerical vs. global pattern understanding) for time series reasoning, but there is no existing method to dynamically select the best modality and model for each query based on task, query characteristics, and cost-performance preferences.
AI.method: TSRouter constructs a heterogeneous graph with task, query, modality, and model nodes to contextualize their interactions, then formulates routing as a candidate scoring problem to evaluate modality-model pairs based on user-defined performance-cost preferences.
AI.result: TSRouter achieves 16% to 46% relative improvements over diverse baselines across 4 time series reasoning tasks, demonstrates robust zero-shot plug-and-play generalization to unseen models and novel tasks, and reduces computational overhead via cost-aware optimization.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic routing between modalities and models based on query context significantly improves time series reasoning efficiency and accuracy, and the graph-based approach generalizes well to unseen scenarios.

title: Multimodal Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to align multimodal large language models (MLLMs), but higher rewards do not always imply better task performance. This risk is amplified when visual evidence is evaluated by text-only or weakly grounded rewards. We study reward hacking in MLLM RL across safety VQA, chart VQA, and stress-test settings, varying reward design, data ambiguity, model scale (2B-32B), and RL algorithm (GRPO, RLOO, DAPO). We introduce Newly Rewarded Failure Rate (NRFR), which measures failures among samples whose proxy reward improves over the SFT baseline. Outcome-only rewards cause severe hacking, reaching 48.1% Reward Hacking Rate (RHR), while NRFR exceeding RHR shows that RL creates new failures rather than merely inheriting them. Scaling reduces but does not eliminate hacking: even the 32B model retains a 54.9% worse rate under outcome-only rewards, whereas answer-aware rewards improve the oracle trend at every scale. Robustness is also algorithm- and scale-dependent: GRPO is consistently most resistant, RLOO remains vulnerable, and DAPO improves substantially from 2B to 8B. Visual-evidence rewards help only with reliable verification: keyword-based checks increase hacking, while VLM-as-judge semantic verification reduces it. Overall, multimodal reward hacking is a systematic result of optimizing imperfect rewards, and robust alignment requires rewards and verifiers that remain reliable under optimization pressure.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies reward hacking in multimodal large language model (MLLM) reinforcement learning, finding that outcome-only rewards cause severe hacking (up to 48.1% RHR), scaling reduces but doesn't eliminate it, GRPO is most robust while RLOO is vulnerable, and visual-evidence rewards help only with reliable semantic verification.
AI.motivation: Higher RL rewards do not always imply better task performance in MLLM alignment, especially when visual evidence is evaluated by text-only or weakly grounded rewards. The risk of reward hacking in multimodal settings is understudied, motivating a systematic investigation.
AI.method: The authors study reward hacking across safety VQA, chart VQA, and stress-test settings, varying reward design, data ambiguity, model scale (2B-32B), and RL algorithm (GRPO, RLOO, DAPO). They introduce Newly Rewarded Failure Rate (NRFR) to measure failures among samples whose proxy reward improves over the SFT baseline.
AI.result: Outcome-only rewards cause severe hacking reaching 48.1% RHR; NRFR exceeding RHR shows RL creates new failures. Scaling reduces hacking but 32B retains 54.9% worse rate under outcome-only rewards. GRPO is most resistant, RLOO vulnerable, DAPO improves from 2B to 8B. Keyword-based visual checks increase hacking, VLM-as-judge semantic verification reduces it.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal reward hacking is a systematic result of optimizing imperfect rewards, and robust alignment requires rewards and verifiers that remain reliable under optimization pressure.

title: Diversifying to Verify: When Task-Equivalent Programs Differ in Verifiability
summary:
Program verification is crucial for software correctness, but producing fully verified programs remains difficult in practice. This paper studies whether implementation structure affects automated verifiability when multiple generated programs are intended to satisfy the same task-level semantics.
  We present Diversify2Verify, a staged LLM-based pipeline for Why3 that infers representation-specific contracts, generates and tests diverse recursive and imperative array/list implementations, and attempts verification with bounded verifier-guided annotation repair. We also construct a verification-oriented benchmark of 73 tasks over integers, arrays, and lists, yielding 292 implementation variants. Diversify2Verify verifies 96 artifacts initially and 154 after two repair passes, improving artifact-level verification from 32.9% to 52.7%. At the task level, at least one variant verifies for 49 of 73 tasks, a 67.1% success rate. These results show that task-equivalent implementations can differ substantially in verifiability and that implementation diversity helps find verification-friendly artifacts.

AI.tldr: Diversify2Verify is a staged LLM-based pipeline that generates diverse implementations from the same task specification and finds that implementation diversity significantly affects automated verifiability, improving verification rates from 32.9% to 52.7% and achieving a 67.1% task-level success rate.
AI.motivation: Program verification is important but difficult; the paper investigates whether the structure of implementations (when multiple programs satisfy the same semantics) affects their automated verifiability.
AI.method: A staged LLM-based pipeline for Why3 that infers contracts, generates diverse recursive and imperative implementations over integers/arrays/lists, and applies bounded verifier-guided annotation repair in two passes.
AI.result: 96 artifacts verified initially, 154 after two repair passes (32.9%→52.7% artifact-level); at least one variant per task verified for 49/73 tasks (67.1% success rate).
AI.conclusion: Task-equivalent implementations vary substantially in verifiability; generating diverse implementations is an effective strategy for finding verification-friendly artifacts.

title: Subtoken Vision Transformer for Fine-grained Recognition
summary: We present Subtoken Vision Transformer (SubViT), a selective image tokenization method for fine-grained visual recognition. Standard Vision Transformers compress each fixed-size patch into a single token, although fine-grained distinctions often depend on localized variations within only a few patches. SubViT addresses this mismatch by representing discriminative patches with multiple subtokens while retaining the original token sequence for global context, thereby allocating additional capacity where it is most needed. Since attention heads encode complementary semantics and extracting attention maps at inference requires an extra backbone forward, we adopt a two-stage training strategy. Stage 1 fine-tunes the ViT using subdivision regions sampled from random attention heads, exposing the model to diverse subdivision patterns. Stage 2 identifies informative attention maps through feature-degradation distances and distills them into a lightweight single-map router, which directly predicts deterministic token-importance scores without a separate attention forward. We evaluate SubViT on Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), a challenging task requiring both fine-grained discrimination and generalization to unlabeled novel categories. Across CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, and Stanford Cars, SubViT improves the average novel-category accuracy of DINOv2 from $81.3\%$ to $84.7\%$, with only $0.50$ ms additional latency and $3.4\%$ more FLOPs, while reducing latency by $73.8\%$ relative to Retina Patch. Results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 demonstrate its broader applicability.

AI.tldr: SubViT introduces selective image tokenization that splits discriminative patches into multiple subtokens for fine-grained recognition, using a two-stage training (random attention heads + distilled lightweight router) to improve GCD accuracy with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Standard ViTs compress each fixed-size patch into a single token, but fine-grained distinctions often depend on localized variations within only a few patches. This mismatch limits recognition performance on fine-grained tasks.
AI.method: SubViT adopts a two-stage training strategy: Stage 1 fine-tunes ViT with subdivision regions sampled from random attention heads; Stage 2 identifies informative attention maps via feature-degradation distances and distills them into a lightweight single-map router that predicts token-importance scores without extra attention forward passes.
AI.result: On CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, and Stanford Cars, SubViT improves DINOv2's average novel-category accuracy from 81.3% to 84.7% with only 0.50 ms additional latency and 3.4% more FLOPs, while reducing latency by 73.8% relative to Retina Patch. Also validated on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100.
AI.conclusion: SubViT effectively addresses the patch-token granularity mismatch for fine-grained visual recognition by selectively allocating more capacity to discriminative regions, achieving strong gains on GCD with minimal computational overhead.

title: Training, Reading, and Editing Legible Transformers
summary: A transformer can be built from operators that are legible by construction -- bounded, named units that read as fuzzy set operations rather than dense activations -- but legibility must be pressed for during training, and the pressure has a failure mode. A crispness penalty meant to sharpen a bounded operator into a decisive detector instead collapses it into a dead constant. An identity, E[v(1-v)] = mu(1-mu) - var, shows why -- the penalty is a variance-minimizer blind to the difference between a live detector and a constant -- and names the fix: a per-channel variance floor, the target legibility metric written as a loss, which recovers both legibility and quality. A learned per-unit fraction then retires the hand-set reserved-GELU partition of prior work: given the choice the model keeps no unit as pure GELU and routes 87% of its load-bearing computation through crisp operators. The result is the most legible transformer we have built -- 78% of its feed-forward operands and 50% of its attention value channels are crisp-and-contextual detectors, and per-head legibility rises from 18% in shallow layers to 78% in deep ones. Read in the correct rotated per-layer frame, these units separate a clean detection (what a unit responds to) from a harder naming (what its output decodes to); and because the objective makes each unit crisp and sparse, edits to them are far more local -- 50-184x in the deep layers where the edit sites concentrate -- and can target explicit conjunctions a single neuron cannot express. Finally, a between-unit decorrelation pressure exposes a legibility dial: it trades a circuit's reuse for independence at no quality cost, turning concepts into single, surgically editable units and a prediction into a short explanation read off a handful of named operations. Quality holds at parity with a conventional baseline throughout.

AI.tldr: A transformer can be made legible by training with a crispness penalty, but this penalty collapses operators into dead constants unless a per-channel variance floor is added. This yields a transformer where 78% of feed-forward and 50% of attention channels are crisp-and-contextual detectors, edits are 50-184x more local, and a decorrelation pressure enables single-unit concepts with no quality loss vs. baseline.
AI.motivation: To build transformers whose internal operations are interpretable by construction — using bounded, named units that read as fuzzy set operations — while maintaining model quality.
AI.method: Identifies a failure mode of crispness penalties (variance minimization collapsing units to constants) via the identity E[v(1-v)] = μ(1-μ) - Var; fixes it with a per-channel variance floor written as a target legibility loss. Adds a learned per-unit fraction to replace hand-set GELU partitions, and a between-unit decorrelation pressure to trade reuse for independence.
AI.result: 78% of feed-forward operands and 50% of attention value channels are crisp-and-contextual detectors; per-head legibility rises from 18% (shallow) to 78% (deep). Edits are 50-184x more local in deep layers. Quality matches conventional baseline.
AI.conclusion: Legible transformers are achievable at no quality cost; the decorrelation pressure provides a "legibility dial" that turns concepts into single editable units and predictions into short explanations from named operations.

title: Shared Selective Persistent Memory for Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Agentic LLM systems that generate code through multi-turn tool use face a fundamental context problem: each session starts from zero, discarding the configuration choices, domain constraints, data schemas, and tool-use patterns that made previous sessions productive. Naively persisting entire conversation histories is token-inefficient and counterproductive: irrelevant context degrades generation quality. We introduce shared selective persistent memory, an architecture that identifies and retains four categories of reusable context (task specifications, data schemas, tool configurations, and output constraints) while discarding session-specific reasoning traces. Crucially, this memory is shared: workspaces encapsulating selective memory can be transferred across users with role-based access control, enabling collaborative reuse without redundant specification. We implement it in a deployed collaborative workspace platform where LLM agents produce, edit, and maintain git-versioned artifacts (dashboards, reports, and data-driven documents) from heterogeneous sources (CSV, SQL, REST APIs, and MCP servers). A complementary zero-token data refresh mechanism decouples generated programs from runtime data, enabling artifact reuse without re-invocation. Across three enterprise scenarios, shared selective persistent memory achieves 96% task completion (vs. 79% without memory and 71% with full history). Zero-token refresh eliminates LLM re-invocation for recurring updates (14x task-time reduction), while summary-driven generation cuts per-invocation token cost by 97x versus raw data injection. A replication on four public datasets confirms generalizability, with zero-token refresh succeeding in 12/12 trials. Notably, naive full-history persistence actively degrades completion by biasing the agent with stale traces, while selective memory outperforms both extremes.

AI.tldr: Introduces shared selective persistent memory for agentic LLM systems, which retains reusable context (task specs, data schemas, tool configs, output constraints) while discarding session-specific traces, achieving 96% task completion and 97x token cost reduction via a collaborative workspace platform with zero-token data refresh.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM systems generating code through multi-turn tool use suffer from a context initialization problem—each session starts from scratch, losing configuration choices, domain constraints, data schemas, and tool-use patterns from prior sessions. Full history persistence is token-inefficient and degrades generation quality due to irrelevant context.
AI.method: Proposes shared selective persistent memory architecture that extracts and retains four reusable context categories (task specifications, data schemas, tool configurations, output constraints) while discarding session-specific reasoning traces. Implemented in a collaborative workspace platform with role-based access control, git-versioned artifacts, and a zero-token data refresh mechanism that decouples generated programs from runtime data.
AI.result: 96% task completion vs. 79% (no memory) and 71% (full history). Zero-token refresh reduces task time by 14x and eliminates LLM re-invocation. Summary-driven generation cuts per-invocation token cost by 97x vs. raw data injection. Replication on 4 public datasets confirms generalizability with 12/12 zero-token refresh success. Full-history persistence actively degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: Selective persistent memory outperforms both no-memory and full-history extremes, demonstrating that structured context retention with session-specific trace pruning is essential for efficient and effective multi-turn agentic code generation, and that zero-token refresh enables reusable artifact maintenance without costly re-invocation.

title: How Do Software Professionals Evaluate AI-Generated Code? (Registered Report)
comment: This report has been accepted for ESEM 2026 (Registered Reports Track)
summary: Recent advances in generative AI tools have significantly changed how software professionals write, evaluate, and interact with code. Generative AI tools such as GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude are increasingly being integrated into everyday workflows. Despite the growing adoption of and reliance on these tools, it remains unclear as to how software professionals evaluate the code they generate. To explore this topic, we will conduct a constructivist grounded theory study that incorporates a survey, semi-structured interviews, and laddering interviews. With the initial survey data collection complete, we aim to interview 20--50 software professionals iteratively until theoretical saturation is achieved. This research aims to build a theory of how software professionals evaluate AI-generated code, grounded in their accounts of evaluative practices, perceptions, and preferences.

AI.tldr: This paper outlines a constructivist grounded theory study investigating how software professionals evaluate AI-generated code from tools like GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude. The study uses surveys, semi-structured interviews, and laddering interviews with 20-50 professionals to build a grounded theory of their evaluative practices, perceptions, and preferences.
AI.motivation: Despite the growing adoption of generative AI tools in software development, there is a lack of understanding about how software professionals evaluate the code these tools produce.
AI.method: Constructivist grounded theory approach incorporating a survey, semi-structured interviews, and laddering interviews with 20-50 software professionals, conducted iteratively until theoretical saturation.
AI.result: Initial survey data collection is complete; the study is ongoing with plans for iterative interviews.
AI.conclusion: The research aims to produce a grounded theory of how software professionals evaluate AI-generated code based on their reported evaluative practices, perceptions, and preferences.

title: DETRAM: End-to-end DEtection, Tracking and Recovery of HumAn Meshes
summary: In the task of human mesh recovery (HMR), multi-person scenes are particularly difficult to handle due to the many entities that appear and occlusions between them over time. In particular for video inputs, there is a need to track each entity reliably and consistently. Existing methods rely on pretrained human detection modules, increasing their runtime and limiting the number of tracked entities. We present DETRAM, a unified framework for multi-person HMR and tracking that simultaneously detects, reconstructs, and tracks humans across time, both automatically and via user prompts. DETRAM uses a single transformer decoder with an identity-consistent set of learnable query embeddings that persist across frames: detection queries discover new people, tracking queries maintain pose and shape for existing individuals, and prompt queries follow user-specified identities. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art tracking results on PoseTrack21, 3DPW, BEDLAM, and MuPoTS-3D, and competitive reconstruction accuracy on BEDLAM and 3DPW, while uniquely supporting prompt-based tracking of individuals in multi-person scenes. To our knowledge, this is the first method to unify promptability and multi-person HMR with tracking in an end-to-end trainable framework, enabling user-directed human analysis in videos.

AI.tldr: DETRAM is a unified transformer-based framework for multi-person human mesh recovery and tracking that simultaneously detects, reconstructs, and tracks humans across video frames using identity-consistent learnable query embeddings, achieving state-of-the-art tracking results while uniquely supporting prompt-based tracking.
AI.motivation: Multi-person human mesh recovery in videos is challenging due to occlusions and the need for consistent tracking. Existing methods rely on pretrained detection modules, which increase runtime and limit the number of trackable entities. There is also a lack of methods that support user-directed (prompt-based) tracking in multi-person HMR.
AI.method: DETRAM uses a single transformer decoder with identity-consistent learnable query embeddings that persist across frames. The query embeddings are categorized into three types: detection queries (discover new people), tracking queries (maintain pose and shape for existing individuals), and prompt queries (follow user-specified identities). This enables simultaneous detection, reconstruction, and tracking in an end-to-end trainable framework.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art tracking results on PoseTrack21, 3DPW, BEDLAM, and MuPoTS-3D, and competitive reconstruction accuracy on BEDLAM and 3DPW. Also uniquely supports prompt-based tracking of individuals in multi-person scenes.
AI.conclusion: DETRAM is the first method to unify promptability and multi-person HMR with tracking in an end-to-end trainable framework, enabling user-directed human analysis in videos without reliance on external detection modules.

title: FairSelect: A Systematic Evaluation of Multi-Level and Intersectional Algorithmic Fairness
comment: 15 pages, 5 tables, Submission to Health Informatics Knowledge Management Conference 2026
summary: Algorithmic fairness methods are increasingly used to identify and mitigate bias in machine learning models, yet most approaches are evaluated in isolation and along single demographic axes. This limits practical guidance for selecting fairness strategies, where disparities may arise across intersectional subgroups and across multiple stages of the modeling lifecycle. This work presents FairSelect, a toolkit for systematically evaluating fairness mitigation strategies applied individually and in combination across preprocessing, inprocessing, and postprocessing stages. FairSelect supports multiple model architectures, intersectional subgroup evaluation, and comparison of fairness utility tradeoffs across baseline, single method, and multi level configurations. The framework was validated using synthetic clinical datasets designed to represent specific bias mechanisms and a real-world replication of two-year stroke risk prediction among patients with atrial fibrillation. Synthetic experiments showed that targeted fairness methods generally reduced intended subgroup disparities, while combined strategies produced larger average fairness improvements with modest utility tradeoffs. In the clinical prediction task, mitigation effects were highly variable, with some combinations improving both fairness and predictive performance while others were ineffective or counterproductive. These findings demonstrate that fairness interventions interact in nonadditive and context dependent ways. FairSelect provides a practical framework for systematically identifying fairness strategies that improve subgroup equity while preserving model performance in clinical machine learning.

AI.tldr: FairSelect is a toolkit for systematically evaluating single and combined fairness mitigation strategies across preprocessing, inprocessing, and postprocessing stages, with intersectional subgroup evaluation. Synthetic experiments showed combined strategies improve fairness with modest utility tradeoffs, while a clinical stroke risk prediction task revealed highly variable, nonadditive effects—some combinations improved both fairness and performance, others were counterproductive.
AI.motivation: Existing fairness methods are evaluated in isolation and along single demographic axes, providing limited practical guidance for selecting strategies when disparities span intersectional subgroups and multiple modeling stages.
AI.method: FairSelect evaluates fairness mitigation strategies individually and in combination across preprocessing, inprocessing, and postprocessing stages, supports multiple architectures and intersectional subgroups, and compares fairness-utility tradeoffs across baseline, single, and multi-level configurations.
AI.result: Synthetic experiments: targeted methods reduced subgroup disparities; combined strategies produced larger average fairness improvements with modest utility tradeoffs. Clinical task: mitigation effects were highly variable—some combinations improved both fairness and performance, others were ineffective or counterproductive.
AI.conclusion: Fairness interventions interact in nonadditive and context-dependent ways. FairSelect provides a practical framework for identifying strategies that improve subgroup equity while preserving model performance in clinical machine learning.

title: SAGEAgent: A Self-Evolving Agent for Cost-Aware Modality Acquisition in Multimodal Survival Prediction
summary: Does every cancer patient truly need a complete diagnostic workup for accurate survival prediction? In multimodal clinical oncology, diagnostic modalities follow a clinically mandated order of escalating burden -- from demographics collected at intake to genomic profiling requiring specialized tissue analysis. Current multimodal survival methods either assume all modalities are available or passively handle missing data, but none actively reason about whether acquiring the next modality is justified for a given patient along this ordered workflow. We formulate this as a sequential decision problem and propose SAGEAgent (Sequential Acquisition Guided by Experience), a self-evolving LLM-based clinical agent that decides which diagnostic modalities to acquire for each patient, balancing predictive accuracy against clinical invasiveness. SAGEAgent reasons about each patient's evolving diagnostic state through clinical tools that translate numerical predictions into text, an episodic memory that retrieves similar past cases, and a semantic memory that accumulates reusable decision patterns from experience. Experiments on a glioma cohort combining TCGA-LGG, TCGA-GBM, and BraTS with four diagnostic modalities demonstrate that SAGEAgent achieves competitive survival prediction accuracy while reducing average acquisition burden by 55%.

AI.tldr: SAGEAgent is an LLM-based clinical agent that sequentially decides which diagnostic modalities to acquire for each cancer patient, reducing acquisition burden by 55% while maintaining competitive survival prediction accuracy on a glioma cohort.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal survival methods either assume all modalities are available or passively handle missing data, but do not actively reason about whether acquiring the next, more invasive diagnostic modality is justified for a given patient along the clinically ordered workflow.
AI.method: Formulates the problem as a sequential decision process and proposes SAGEAgent, a self-evolving LLM-based agent using clinical tools (translating numerical predictions to text), episodic memory (retrieving similar past cases), and semantic memory (accumulating reusable decision patterns) to decide which modalities to acquire per patient.
AI.result: On a glioma cohort combining TCGA-LGG, TCGA-GBM, and BraTS with four diagnostic modalities, SAGEAgent achieves competitive survival prediction accuracy while reducing average acquisition burden by 55%.
AI.conclusion: Not all patients require a complete diagnostic workup for accurate survival prediction; selectively acquiring modalities guided by an intelligent agent can significantly reduce clinical burden without sacrificing prediction quality.

title: Practical Source Code Recovery from Binary Functions Using Anchor-Based Retrieval and LLM Reasoning
summary: We present a practical pipeline for recovering source code from stripped binary functions by combining reverse engineering, anchor-based source code retrieval, and large language model reasoning. Our binary-to-source-code retrieval method attempts to identify the source function from a source code database, rather than generating approximate decompiled pseudocode. It extracts anchors such as strings, constants, external calls, and available function names using Ghidra, retrieves candidate files via an inverted-index search database, narrows candidates to likely function snippets, and re-ranks them with a large language model (LLM) based on disassembly, decompiled code, and source metadata. Confident matches can also serve as anchors in later passes. In an evaluation backed by our high-fidelity source code database on a stripped, optimized tcpdump binary, our proposed binary-to-source matching method achieves 95.2% assembly instruction coverage. Experiments on a GitHub-based retrieval database showed lower performance with 35.5% instruction coverage on average, mainly due to retrieval misses. These results show that source-level binary recovery excels with high-quality databases and remains a useful tool in noisy environments.

AI.tldr: A pipeline that recovers source code from stripped binaries by combining reverse engineering, anchor-based retrieval from a source database, and LLM re-ranking, achieving 95.2% instruction coverage on a high-fidelity database but only 35.5% on noisy GitHub data.
AI.motivation: To recover exact source code from stripped binary functions, moving beyond decompiled pseudocode by leveraging existing source databases and retrieval techniques.
AI.method: Uses Ghidra to extract anchors (strings, constants, external calls, function names), searches an inverted-index database for candidate files, narrows to function snippets, and re-ranks with an LLM based on disassembly, decompiled code, and metadata. Confident matches serve as anchors in iterative passes.
AI.result: 95.2% assembly instruction coverage on stripped, optimized tcpdump with a high-fidelity database; 35.5% average instruction coverage on GitHub-based retrieval database due to retrieval misses.
AI.conclusion: Source-level binary recovery excels with high-quality databases and remains useful even in noisy environments with lower-quality databases.

title: Beyond Time Shifts: Adapting Omni-LLM as a Reference-Free Evaluator for Generative Audio-Visual Models
summary: As audio-visual generative models evolve into world simulators, cross-modal synchronization stands as a critical proxy for assessing the consistency of world dynamics and causality in generated content. However, existing evaluation metrics presume structural correctness, reducing synchronization to mere temporal alignment. Consequently, they fail on generative outputs, especially when exhibiting structural hallucinations and asymmetric cross-modal relations, which currently \textbf{mandate expert human annotation to assess synchronization.} This dependency introduces a critical paradox: \emph{human evaluators rely on relative, reference-dependent comparisons, whereas automated metrics require reference-free, absolute scalars.} We resolve this paradox by proposing a framework that distills relative human perception into a continuous, globally consistent metric. First, we introduce SynthSync, a dataset of generative failures ranked via pairwise human annotations. Second, we adapt the Omni-LLM equipped with a continuous latent projection to translate relative human rankings into continuous absolute values. Third, we propose Real-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization ($\mathbb{R}$-GRPO) to internalize the global causal structure of synchronization via listwise score distributions. Empirically, our metric achieves state-of-the-art human preference alignment. We leverage this estimator to establish a standardized benchmark, advancing AV-Gen assessment from low-level signal correlation to visually grounded causality.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the paradox between relative human evaluation and absolute automated metrics for assessing cross-modal synchronization in audio-visual generative models. The authors propose SynthSync (a dataset of generative failures with pairwise human rankings), adapt an Omni-LLM with continuous latent projection to translate relative rankings into absolute scores, and introduce Real-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization (R-GRPO) to internalize global causal structure via listwise score distributions. The resulting metric achieves state-of-the-art human preference alignment and establishes a standardized benchmark for AV-Gen assessment.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics for audio-visual synchronization assume structural correctness and reduce synchronization to temporal alignment, failing on generative outputs that exhibit structural hallucinations and asymmetric cross-modal relations. This forces reliance on expert human annotation, creating a paradox: human evaluators provide relative, reference-dependent comparisons, but automated metrics require reference-free, absolute scalars.
AI.method: 1) SynthSync: a dataset of generative failures with pairwise human annotations. 2) Omni-LLM adapted with continuous latent projection to map relative human rankings to continuous absolute values. 3) Real-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization (R-GRPO) to internalize global causal structure via listwise score distributions.
AI.result: State-of-the-art human preference alignment; establishes a standardized benchmark advancing AV-Gen assessment from low-level signal correlation to visually grounded causality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully bridges the gap between relative human perception and absolute automated metrics for evaluating cross-modal synchronization in audio-visual generative models, enabling reference-free, globally consistent assessment that aligns with human judgment.

title: Eluna: An Agentic LLM System for Automating Warehouse Operations with Reasoning and Task Execution
summary: Warehouse operations are governed by Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that encode complex, multi-system decision logic, which must be executed reliably under strict time constraints, yet LLM agents lack mechanisms to enforce procedural compliance and degrade under the context overload full SOP specifications introduce. We present Eluna, a production-deployed agentic system for reliable SOP execution. Eluna is a graph-guided, multi-agent framework that encodes SOPs as directed acyclic graphs with progressive disclosure and delegates independent tasks to parallel sub-agents, each with persistent code execution and live data access. To meet production latency and accuracy needs, we use asymmetric episodic distillation where a strong teacher is improved through episodic error memories, then a smaller student is fine-tuned on the corrected trajectories with memory stripped, internalizing corrections without inference-time overhead. On a 13-task benchmark and two production applications, our fine-tuned models match or exceed their teacher, beat all larger off-the-shelf baselines, and reach 94% expert agreement on the ticket processing application.

AI.tldr: Eluna is a production-deployed, graph-guided multi-agent framework that encodes SOPs as DAGs with progressive disclosure, uses asymmetric episodic distillation to fine-tune a smaller student model on corrected teacher trajectories, achieving 94% expert agreement on ticket processing while meeting production latency/accuracy requirements.
AI.motivation: LLM agents lack mechanisms to enforce procedural compliance with complex SOPs and degrade under context overload when full SOP specifications are introduced, yet warehouse operations require reliable execution under strict time constraints.
AI.method: Eluna encodes SOPs as directed acyclic graphs with progressive disclosure, delegates tasks to parallel sub-agents with persistent code execution and live data access, and uses asymmetric episodic distillation (strong teacher improved via episodic error memories, then smaller student fine-tuned on corrected trajectories with memory stripped).
AI.result: On a 13-task benchmark and two production applications, the fine-tuned models match or exceed their teacher, beat all larger off-the-shelf baselines, and reach 94% expert agreement on the ticket processing application.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric episodic distillation with graph-guided multi-agent decomposition enables reliable, low-latency SOP execution in production, with student models internalizing corrections without inference-time overhead.

title: Beyond Fixed Representations: The Vocabulary and Verifier Gaps in Open-Ended AI
summary:
Modern AI systems are increasingly being evaluated for their ability to reason, code, prove theorems, use tools, and long-horizon research tasks. These are powerful capabilities, but they share a structural limitation: the representational frame within which the model operates, including its conceptual vocabulary, the space of admissible solutions it can search, and the criteria by which success is evaluated, is typically fixed and supplied in advance. This paper argues that building stronger intelligent systems capable of open-ended innovation requires additional classes of operations: the creation, stabilization, and reuse of new representational primitives, which alter the space being searched rather than simply searching within it.
  We characterize the distance between current AI systems and genuinely open-ended intelligence through two gaps. The first is the vocabulary gap, the difficulty of inventing and stabilizing new representational primitives rather than merely recombining existing ones. The second is the verifier gap, the difficulty of judging the value of a new primitive when its full payoff may be visible only after future reuse. We interpret both gaps through a unified framework of intelligence as cognitive discrepancy reduction. By viewing intelligent behaviors as a sequence of cognitive transformations, we distinguish intra-space transformations which operate within a fixed representational frame, from generative transformations which may modify the frame itself. On this basis, we propose a ladder of innovation autonomy and outline several directions for advancing open-ended AI, including objectives that reward useful representational change, persistent memory architectures for invented primitives, and adaptive verification mechanisms capable of evolving alongside the representations they evaluate.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that current AI systems operate within fixed representational frames, limiting open-ended innovation. It identifies two gaps—vocabulary and verifier—that separate today's AI from truly open-ended intelligence, and proposes a framework of cognitive discrepancy reduction with a ladder of innovation autonomy to guide progress.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems excel at reasoning, coding, theorem proving, and tool use but are fundamentally limited by operating within fixed representational frames. The paper argues that genuine open-ended innovation requires the ability to create, stabilize, and reuse new representational primitives that alter the search space itself, rather than merely searching within it.
AI.method: The paper characterizes the gap through two specific challenges: the vocabulary gap (inventing new representational primitives vs. recombining existing ones) and the verifier gap (judging value of new primitives when payoff depends on future reuse). It unifies these through a framework of "intelligence as cognitive discrepancy reduction," distinguishing intra-space (fixed frame) from generative (frame-modifying) transformations, and proposes a ladder of innovation autonomy.
AI.result: The main result is the articulation of two fundamental gaps (vocabulary and verifier) limiting current AI, a unified theoretical framework distinguishing intra-space vs. generative transformations, and a proposed ladder of innovation autonomy for categorizing AI systems by their capacity for open-ended innovation.
AI.conclusion: Advancing open-ended AI requires: (1) objectives that reward useful representational change, (2) persistent memory architectures for storing invented primitives, and (3) adaptive verification mechanisms that evolve alongside the representations they evaluate. These directions aim to bridge the vocabulary and verifier gaps toward genuinely open-ended intelligence.

title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly deployed to autonomously perform software engineering tasks in terminal-based environments, making their reliability a growing concern. Existing empirical studies investigate why coding agents fail, yet they largely treat failure as a final outcome rather than a temporal process, providing limited insight into how failures emerge, evolve, and become unrecoverable. We present the first large-scale empirical study of CLI coding-agent failure trajectories, introducing a process-oriented framework that analyzes failure through its onset, evolution, and recovery across execution trajectories. We first collect 3,843 execution trajectories generated by seven frontier models across three coding-agent scaffolds (OpenHands, MiniSWE, and Terminus2) on Terminal-Bench, then carefully filter them to obtain 1,794 complete and valid trajectories for manual annotation (over 63,000 execution steps), from which we derive 14 findings spanning failure occurrence, root causes, recovery, and cross-system consistency. Our findings show that coding-agent failures are predominantly driven by epistemic errors, typically begin within the first few execution steps, and often remain hidden until recovery is no longer possible, suggesting that improving coding-agent reliability requires earlier validation and intervention rather than relying solely on final-outcome evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study of coding-agent failure trajectories, analyzing 1,794 manually annotated trajectories (63,000+ steps) from 7 models across 3 scaffolds on Terminal-Bench. It finds that failures are predominantly epistemic, occur early, and remain hidden until unrecoverable, advocating for earlier validation.
AI.motivation: Existing studies treat coding-agent failures as final outcomes rather than temporal processes, providing limited insight into how failures emerge, evolve, and become unrecoverable.
AI.method: Collected 3,843 execution trajectories from 7 frontier models across 3 coding-agent scaffolds (OpenHands, MiniSWE, Terminus2) on Terminal-Bench, filtered to 1,794 complete trajectories for manual annotation (63,000+ steps), deriving 14 findings across failure occurrence, root causes, recovery, and cross-system consistency.
AI.result: Coding-agent failures are predominantly driven by epistemic errors, typically begin within the first few execution steps, and often remain hidden until recovery is no longer possible.
AI.conclusion: Improving coding-agent reliability requires earlier validation and intervention rather than relying solely on final-outcome evaluation.

title: A Coreset Selection Framework with Ensemble Aggregation for Image Classification
summary: The rapid growth of image data has produced large-scale datasets, raising concerns about the time and memory costs of model training. Selecting representative training subsets, however, remains challenging: individual sample contributions are unclear, and model behavior varies across datasets and runs. We address these challenges with a framework that combines coreset selection with an ensemble aggregation over multiple runs. For coreset selection, we propose SCOre-Stratified Selection (SCOSS), which partitions the training data into intervals based on a chosen score and samples from each interval. The ensemble combines predictions from multiple runs, each performed on an independently sampled training subset. As baselines, we use moderate and random selection, each in original and class-balanced versions. We assess the framework with Simple Graph Convolution (SGC) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers under different sampling ratios. Experiments show that SCOSS is competitive with baselines, often the best choice for SGC, and enables favorable trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. On the fine-grained dataset, SGC with SCOSS outperforms SVMs when using fewer labeled samples. The code and supplementary materials are publicly available at http://scoss.lucasvalem.com.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SCOSS, a coreset selection framework that partitions training data by score intervals and samples from each, combined with ensemble aggregation across multiple runs. It shows competitive accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, especially for SGC classifiers.
AI.motivation: Large-scale image datasets cause high time and memory costs during training. Selecting representative subsets is difficult because individual sample contributions are unclear and model behavior varies across datasets and runs.
AI.method: A framework combining coreset selection (SCOSS: SCOre-Stratified Selection) with ensemble aggregation over multiple runs. SCOSS partitions training data into intervals based on a chosen score and samples from each. Ensemble combines predictions from multiple runs on independently sampled subsets. Compared against moderate/random selection with class-balanced variants using SGC and SVM classifiers.
AI.result: SCOSS is competitive with baselines, often the best choice for SGC classifiers, and enables favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. On fine-grained datasets, SGC+SCOSS outperforms SVMs with fewer labeled samples.
AI.conclusion: SCOSS provides an effective coreset selection strategy that reduces training costs while maintaining or improving accuracy, particularly well-suited for SGC classifiers and fine-grained classification tasks.

title: NL-PAC: Specification Ambiguity and Certified Minimax Risk Floors in LLM-Mediated Supervision
summary: Large language models increasingly provide labels, evaluations, and feedback for tasks specified in natural language. When a specification admits multiple readings but the supervision channel does not reveal which is operative, additional labels reduce sampling error without resolving the resulting identification problem. We introduce Natural Language PAC (NL-PAC), a framework that uses a fixed model's thresholded decoding law to define admissible labels and candidate targets. The probability that multiple labels are admissible equals the diameter of the pointwise-admissible target class, and under target-blind supervision every learner incurs worst-case risk of at least half this diameter, at every sample size; the exact randomized minimax risk over this class is attained by a data-independent strategy. Finite-sample confidence bounds make these quantities certifiable from held-out unlabeled inputs. In a frozen Qwen~2.5--3B audit, one prespecified prompt yields a positive model-relative certificate, whereas a paraphrase and exact-rule controls yield zero. A held-out bridge audit finds that supplied candidate reading clauses fail the admissibility condition needed to transfer the certificate to coherent readings. The guarantee is specific to the audited model, prompt, threshold, and input distribution; extending it to human interpretations requires external validation.

AI.tldr: Introduces NL-PAC, a framework for certifying label admissibility in LLMs under ambiguous specifications, showing that model-relative guarantees are specific to the audited model and do not transfer to human interpretations without external validation.
AI.motivation: When a specification admits multiple readings but the supervision channel does not reveal which is operative, additional labels reduce sampling error without resolving the resulting identification problem.
AI.method: NL-PAC uses a fixed model's thresholded decoding law to define admissible labels and candidate targets; probability that multiple labels are admissible equals the diameter of the pointwise-admissible target class; target-blind supervision yields worst-case risk of at least half this diameter; exact randomized minimax risk attained by data-independent strategy; finite-sample confidence bounds make quantities certifiable from held-out unlabeled inputs.
AI.result: In a frozen Qwen 2.5–3B audit, one prespecified prompt yields a positive model-relative certificate, whereas a paraphrase and exact-rule controls yield zero. A held-out bridge audit finds that supplied candidate reading clauses fail the admissibility condition needed to transfer the certificate to coherent readings.
AI.conclusion: The guarantee is specific to the audited model, prompt, threshold, and input distribution; extending it to human interpretations requires external validation.

title: Knowledge Graphs and Explainable AI as Complementary Resources for Urban Mining
comment: Accepted for presentation at the AISE Workshop @ IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: Pre-demolition assessment, the regulated audit process at the heart of urban mining, is an information process in which AI support must serve qualified auditors who remain accountable for the decisions taken. The relevant unit of value is not prediction accuracy alone, but the defensibility of the supported decisions: their legibility, plausibility, sourcing, and contestability. Explainable AI techniques and domain knowledge graphs each address parts of this requirement, and existing taxonomies have catalogued their integration. The literature is descriptively rich but structurally under-specified: what remains less developed is a structural account of why specific integrations produce artefacts neither resource can provide alone. This paper offers a complementarity-theoretic interpretation grounded in the IS resource-based tradition. We propose four consolidated KG-XAI integration modes (Lifting, Constraining, Typing, and Revising), each defined as a typed operation over XAI artefacts and knowledge-graph substrate structures. Each mode unlocks a distinct property of defensibility and contributes to the kind of regulatory artefact pre-demolition assessment demands. A fire-door example from the urban-mining process illustrates the modes using the W3C Linked Building Data stack and valuation extensions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a complementarity-theoretic framework integrating Explainable AI (XAI) and Knowledge Graphs (KG) for defensible pre-demolition assessment in urban mining. Four KG-XAI integration modes (Lifting, Constraining, Typing, Revising) are defined, each targeting a distinct property of defensibility (legibility, plausibility, sourcing, contestability). A fire-door example using W3C Linked Building Data demonstrates the approach.
AI.motivation: Current AI support for pre-demolition assessment focuses on prediction accuracy, but the regulatory context demands defensible decisions (legibility, plausibility, sourcing, contestability). Existing KG-XAI integration literature is descriptively rich but lacks a structural account of why specific integrations yield benefits neither resource alone can provide.
AI.method: The paper develops a complementarity-theoretic interpretation grounded in the IS resource-based tradition. It proposes four consolidated KG-XAI integration modes—Lifting, Constraining, Typing, and Revising—each defined as a typed operation over XAI artefacts and knowledge-graph substrate structures. A fire-door example from urban mining illustrates the modes using the W3C Linked Building Data stack and valuation extensions.
AI.result: Four distinct KG-XAI integration modes are identified, each unlocking a specific property of defensibility. The framework provides a structural account of complementarity between KGs and XAI, moving beyond descriptive taxonomies to explain why specific integrations produce artefacts neither resource alone can provide.
AI.conclusion: The complementarity-theoretic framework structurally explains KG-XAI integration for defensible regulatory decision support in pre-demolition assessment. The four modes offer a principled basis for designing AI-augmented audit processes where accountability and defensibility are paramount.

title: Balancing Usefulness and Naturalness: An LLM-based Curation Pipeline for Code Review Comments
comment: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2502.03425
summary:
Code review is a cornerstone of software development, where reviewers provide feedback through written comments to ensure code quality, maintainability, and correctness. The effectiveness of this process hinges on the quality of review comments. As large language models (LLMs) gain traction in automating code review tasks, the utility of these systems is directly limited by the quality of the datasets on which they are trained. Unfortunately, existing code review datasets are often noisy, inconsistent, or poorly structured, which hinders the ability of LLMs to learn to generate accurate, helpful, and human-like review comments.
  To overcome these limitations, we propose two different curation pipelines designed to improve both the quality and the utility of large-scale code review datasets. In the first pipeline, all review comments are systematically reformulated by an LLM to improve their clarity, conciseness, and civility while preserving their semantic intent. The curated dataset resulting from this approach, called CuREV, offers cleaner, higher-quality, and easier-to-learn-from comments that lead to measurable improvements in downstream automation tasks, namely review comment generation and code refinement. Building on this, we propose an improved pipeline, guided by high-quality exemplars, that enhances the realism and diversity of curated review comments. This method first separates the dataset into high-quality and low-quality reviews, based on a systematic quality assessment using an evaluation framework. High-quality comments are preserved in their original form and further used as in-context exemplars to inspire the reformulation of low-quality comments. By varying the exemplars provided, the reformulated comments are not only clearer and more actionable but also exhibit a broader range of writing styles, making them more realistic and human-like.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two curation pipelines to improve code review datasets for LLM training: CuREV (systematic LLM reformulation of all comments) and an enhanced exemplar-guided pipeline that separates high/low-quality comments, using high-quality ones as in-context examples to reformulate low-quality ones, resulting in more realistic, diverse, and human-like review comments.
AI.motivation: Existing code review datasets are noisy, inconsistent, and poorly structured, which limits the ability of LLMs to generate accurate, helpful, and human-like review comments.
AI.method: Two curation pipelines: (1) CuREV - systematically reformulates all review comments using an LLM to improve clarity, conciseness, and civility while preserving semantic intent; (2) An improved pipeline that first separates high-quality and low-quality reviews via a systematic quality assessment framework, preserves high-quality comments in original form and uses them as in-context exemplars to inspire reformulation of low-quality comments, varying exemplars to increase diversity and realism.
AI.result: CuREV produces cleaner, higher-quality comments that lead to measurable improvements in downstream tasks (review comment generation and code refinement). The exemplar-guided pipeline produces comments that are clearer, more actionable, and exhibit broader writing styles, making them more realistic and human-like.
AI.conclusion: Both pipelines improve dataset quality and utility for training LLMs in code review automation, with the exemplar-guided approach yielding more diverse and realistic comments.

title: Equivariant Filter for High Performance Image Tracking using an Event Camera
summary: Image tracking is the problem of estimating the transformation that relates a moving image of a scene to an original reference image. The problem is important in control of autonomous vehicles or robots, where the image encodes information about the motion of the camera or environment, as well as in pure computer vision applications. In this paper, we present an equivariant filter design for high performance tracking of planar image transformations using an event camera. The design exploits the Asynchronous Event Blob (AEB) tracker (Wang et al., 2024) to extract feature-position measurements from the raw event stream, and an equivariant filter to compute an affine image translation and rotation using the special Euclidean group symmetry.
