summary: Large-scale autonomous-driving datasets contain vast numbers of recorded scenarios, creating a need for efficient retrieval methods that can identify situations similar to a given query. Existing approaches typically rely on either visual representations or motion-based descriptions, making it difficult to understand their relative strengths and limitations for scenario retrieval. In this work, we present a multimodal framework for autonomous-driving scenario retrieval that combines visual and trajectory-based representations within a unified retrieval pipeline. We investigate two trajectory-based approaches: Exo-Trajectory, an explicit matching method based on surrounding-agent motion, and ScenarioFormer, a transformer-based representation learned from object trajectories using contrastive learning. We compare these approaches against strong vision-based baselines and analyze their behavior across a diverse set of driving scenarios. Experimental results show that trajectory representations provide strong retrieval performance for motion-centric events such as cut-ins, turning maneuvers, and traffic queueing, while visual embeddings excel when appearance cues are informative. Most importantly, combining visual and trajectory information consistently improves retrieval quality, yielding the best overall performance. These findings demonstrate that appearance and motion capture are complementary notions of scenario similarity and motivate multimodal retrieval systems for autonomous-driving data mining, dataset curation, and scenario-based validation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multimodal framework for autonomous-driving scenario retrieval that combines visual and trajectory-based representations. Trajectory methods excel at motion-centric events (cut-ins, turns, queueing), visual embeddings excel when appearance cues matter, and combining them consistently yields the best performance, demonstrating that appearance and motion are complementary for scenario similarity.
AI.motivation: Large-scale autonomous-driving datasets contain vast scenario records, but existing retrieval methods rely on either visual or motion-based descriptions alone, making it unclear how they compare. A unified understanding of their relative strengths and limitations is needed for efficient scenario retrieval.
AI.method: The authors present a multimodal retrieval framework combining visual and trajectory-based representations. Two trajectory approaches are explored: Exo-Trajectory (explicit matching of surrounding-agent motion) and ScenarioFormer (transformer-based contrastive learning on object trajectories). These are compared against strong vision-based baselines across diverse driving scenarios.
AI.result: Trajectory representations excel at motion-centric events (cut-ins, turning, queueing); visual embeddings perform best when appearance cues are informative. Combining visual and trajectory information consistently yields the best overall retrieval quality.
AI.conclusion: Appearance and motion capture are complementary notions of scenario similarity, motivating multimodal retrieval systems for autonomous-driving data mining, dataset curation, and scenario-based validation.

title: Forget Narrowly, Retain Broadly: Unlearning as an Asymmetric Generalization Problem
summary: Machine unlearning in LLMs is the targeted removal of specific knowledge while preserving all other capabilities, critical for privacy and safety. Yet existing benchmarks measure it unreliably. They miss knowledge that resurfaces under paraphrased or indirect queries, a failure we call under-forgetting, and lack the semantic, syntactic, and lexical probes needed to verify that unrelated knowledge is preserved, a failure we call over-forgetting. Both failures reflect an asymmetric generalization problem. Forget evaluation must cover diverse query formulations of the same target facts, testing whether forgetting holds beyond exact training prompts. Retain evaluation must probe a far larger and implicitly defined set, namely every fact disjoint from the forget target. The retain set thus defines the effective forget set, yet current datasets provide no fine-grained annotation of this forget-retain boundary. We address this with SUITE, an evaluation protocol and training corpus that captures forget-retain structure for real-world factual domains. Methods trained on SUITE improve substantially, showing that training data is as important as algorithmic design. Building on the obtained insights, we introduce JensUn++, an unlearning algorithm that achieves the best forget-retain utility trade-off across three LLMs, in both sequential and joint unlearning settings. Code and datasets are available at https://amitpeleg.github.io/forget-narrowly-retain-broadly

AI.tldr: SUITE is a new evaluation protocol and training corpus for LLM unlearning that addresses asymmetric generalization—testing diverse query formulations to detect under-forgetting and probing unrelated knowledge to detect over-forgetting—along with JensUn++, an unlearning algorithm achieving the best forget-retain trade-off.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for machine unlearning in LLMs are unreliable: they miss knowledge that resurfaces under paraphrased queries (under-forgetting) and lack sufficient probes to verify unrelated knowledge is preserved (over-forgetting), both reflecting an asymmetric generalization problem.
AI.method: The authors propose SUITE, an evaluation protocol and training corpus that captures fine-grained forget-retain structure for real-world factual domains. They also develop JensUn++, an unlearning algorithm designed to optimize the forget-retain utility trade-off.
AI.result: Methods trained on SUITE show substantial improvement, demonstrating that training data is as important as algorithmic design. JensUn++ achieves the best forget-retain utility trade-off across three LLMs in both sequential and joint unlearning settings.
AI.conclusion: Proper evaluation of LLM unlearning requires diverse query formulations for forget set testing and broad probing for retain set verification; SUITE enables this, and JensUn++ delivers state-of-the-art unlearning performance.

title: Parameter-Efficient Vision-Language Adaptation with Continuous Metadata Conditioning for Animal Re-Identification
comment: This is the author's version of the paper accepted for publication in Expert Systems with Applications. The final authenticated version will be available from the publisher
summary: Long-term animal re-identification (ReID) must remain robust to gradual morphological evolution and seasonal appearance shifts. Although recent vision-language models provide strong pretrained visual representations, adapting them to longitudinal ecological settings remains challenging, particularly under identity and temporal distribution shifts. We present a parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation framework for animal ReID and introduce a continuous metadata-conditioning mechanism that incorporates numerical attributes directly into the prompt representation during training. While low-rank visual adaptation, prompt-based supervision, and cross-modal alignment provide the adaptation framework, the proposed metadata-conditioning strategy constitutes the primary methodological contribution. By preserving the continuous structure of numerical metadata rather than discretizing it into textual categories, the proposed approach enables smooth modulation of the embedding space during training while maintaining a purely visual inference pipeline. Experiments on a seven-year longitudinal fish dataset and multiple wildlife benchmarks demonstrate improved performance under closed-set, open-set, and time-aware evaluation protocols. The results demonstrate that continuous metadata conditioning improves robustness to longitudinal appearance variation and temporal distribution shifts, while parameter-efficient adaptation enables a purely visual inference pipeline without requiring metadata at test time. Code and evaluation splits can be found at: https://github.com/AnilOsmanTur/MetaPrompt-ReID.

AI.tldr: A parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation framework with continuous metadata conditioning (MetaPrompt-ReID) for long-term animal re-identification, enabling robustness to morphological and seasonal changes while maintaining purely visual inference at test time.
AI.motivation: Long-term animal re-identification must handle gradual morphological evolution and seasonal appearance shifts. Adapting vision-language models like CLIP to longitudinal ecological settings is challenging due to identity and temporal distribution shifts, and existing approaches discretize numerical metadata into textual categories, losing continuous structure.
AI.method: Proposes a CLIP adaptation framework with: (1) low-rank visual adaptation, (2) prompt-based supervision, (3) cross-modal alignment, and (4) a continuous metadata-conditioning mechanism that incorporates numerical attributes directly into prompt representations during training, preserving continuous structure rather than discretizing into textual categories.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines on a seven-year longitudinal fish dataset and multiple wildlife benchmarks under closed-set, open-set, and time-aware evaluation protocols; continuous metadata conditioning improves robustness to longitudinal appearance variation and temporal distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Continuous metadata conditioning enhances robustness to temporal appearance shifts; parameter-efficient adaptation enables purely visual inference at test time without requiring metadata, making it practical for deployment in long-term ecological monitoring.

title: LionVote: Per-Layer Learning Rate Adaptation for Lion
summary: Per-layer diagnostics reveal that, at the prescribed learning rate, Lion's effective scale is 2.6-2.8x too high for attention and MLP parameters and ~2x too high for normalization layers on ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100; this 32% cross-layer-type disparity cannot be reproduced by a single global rate. The measurement comes from LionVote, a per-layer learning rate mechanism in which each parameter tensor maintains a compound level, a persistent integer updated every c epochs by two diagnostics (gradient direction stability and momentum health) resolved by a validation loss tiebreaker. Voting thresholds derive from geometric identities, the EMA time constant, and a noise-floor estimate; cadence is bounded structurally and selected by ablation. On ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100, LionVote achieves 69.7% top-1 accuracy vs. Lion's 69.0% (p < 0.02, Welch's t-test) and AdamW's 68.8%. Per-layer adaptation value depends on both architectural heterogeneity and task; on uniform CNN architectures tuned SGD with cosine annealing remains dominant, and on ViT architectures gains are task-dependent.

AI.tldr: LionVote is a per-layer learning rate mechanism that adjusts Lion's effective scale per parameter tensor using two diagnostics (gradient direction stability and momentum health) resolved by validation loss tiebreaker. On ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100, it improves top-1 accuracy from 69.0% (Lion) and 68.8% (AdamW) to 69.7% (p < 0.02), but gains depend on architectural heterogeneity and task.
AI.motivation: Lion's fixed global learning rate creates cross-layer-type disparities (e.g., 2.6-2.8x too high for attention/MLP vs. ~2x for normalization layers), which a single global rate cannot correct.
AI.method: LionVote: each parameter tensor maintains a compound level (persistent integer) updated every c epochs by gradient direction stability and momentum health diagnostics, resolved by validation loss tiebreaker. Voting thresholds derived from geometric identities, EMA time constant, and noise-floor estimate; cadence bounded structurally and selected by ablation.
AI.result: ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100: LionVote 69.7% vs. Lion 69.0% (p < 0.02) vs. AdamW 68.8%. Per-layer adaptation value depends on architectural heterogeneity and task; uniform CNNs with tuned SGD/cosine annealing remain dominant, ViT gains task-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Per-layer learning rate adaptation (LionVote) provides statistically significant improvements over Lion and AdamW on vision transformers, but its value is conditional on architectural heterogeneity and task characteristics.

title: Robustifying Vision-Language Models via Test-Time Prompt Adaptation
summary: Pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP achieve strong zero-shot generalization, but their performance degrades sharply under adversarial perturbations. Existing test-time adaptation methods typically rely on sample-level confidence heuristics, overlooking the intrinsic distributional structure of the data. This sample-centric approach limits robustness, as it fails to distinguish confident adversarial mispredictions from true semantic consistency. In this work, we observe that adversarial distortion is structurally brittle: while holistic representations are corrupted, semantic integrity is often preserved in the distribution of augmented views. Motivated by this insight, we propose RITA, a Robust test-tIme prompt-TAdaptation framework that shifts from sample-level estimates to distribution-level alignment. Specifically, RITA employs optimal transport to align the distribution of augmented visual features with textual prototypes, mitigating adversarial outliers and rectifying cross-modal semantic misalignment. Furthermore, we introduce a dynamic cache to progressively accumulate reliable cues from the test stream for online refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RITA significantly improves adversarial robustness without compromising clean accuracy.

AI.tldr: RITA is a test-time prompt adaptation framework that uses distribution-level alignment via optimal transport (instead of sample-level heuristics) to improve the adversarial robustness of pre-trained VLMs like CLIP, without sacrificing clean accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time adaptation methods rely on sample-level confidence heuristics that fail to distinguish confident adversarial mispredictions from true semantic consistency, limiting robustness.
AI.method: RITA shifts from sample-level estimates to distribution-level alignment by: (1) using optimal transport to align the distribution of augmented visual features with textual prototypes, mitigating adversarial outliers; (2) introducing a dynamic cache for progressive accumulation of reliable cues from the test stream for online refinement.
AI.result: RITA significantly improves adversarial robustness without compromising clean accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial distortion is structurally brittle — holistic representations are corrupted but semantic integrity is preserved in the distribution of augmented views — motivating distribution-level alignment as a more robust test-time adaptation strategy.

title: Autoregressive latent diffusion for 3D molecule generation
summary: Three-dimensional (3D) molecule generation has been dominated by diffusion models, which achieve strong generation quality but typically require the molecular size to be specified a priori. Recent autoregressive approaches have substantially narrowed the performance gap while naturally supporting variable-length generation and conditioning on partial molecular context. However, balancing unconditional and context-conditioned generation remains challenging. We introduce KRONOS, a latent autoregressive diffusion framework that generates molecules in the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder, jointly modeling molecular graph topology and geometry, while retaining the flexibility of autoregressive generation. We further introduce a mixed training strategy inspired by Fill-in-the Middle (FIM) paradigm, enabling both unconditional and fragment-conditioned molecular generation within a single left-to-right autoregressive model. Experiments on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs demonstrate that KRONOS achieves leading unconditional generation performance among autoregressive methods, while remaining competitive with diffusion models. Moreover, fragment-conditioned generation is achieved with negligible impact on unconditional generation performance, demonstrating that both generation paradigms can be supported within a single architecture.

AI.tldr: KRONOS is a latent autoregressive diffusion framework that generates 3D molecules in a latent space, using a Fill-in-the-Middle training strategy to support both unconditional and fragment-conditioned generation in a single model, achieving competitive results with diffusion models on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D molecule generation methods either require pre-specified molecular sizes (diffusion models) or struggle to balance unconditional and context-conditioned generation (autoregressive models). The goal is to create a single framework that supports both generation paradigms flexibly.
AI.method: KRONOS uses a pre-trained autoencoder to map molecules into a latent space, then applies an autoregressive diffusion model in that latent space to jointly model molecular graph topology and geometry. A mixed training strategy inspired by Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) paradigm enables both unconditional and fragment-conditioned generation within a single left-to-right autoregressive model.
AI.result: On QM9 and GEOM-Drugs benchmarks, KRONOS achieves leading unconditional generation performance among autoregressive methods and remains competitive with diffusion models. Fragment-conditioned generation is achieved with negligible impact on unconditional generation performance.
AI.conclusion: Both unconditional and fragment-conditioned molecular generation can be effectively supported within a single autoregressive architecture, demonstrating flexibility without sacrificing generation quality.

title: Hydra++: Real-Time Hierarchical 3D Scene Graph Construction With Object-Level Shape Estimation
comment: 8 pages, 12 figures, accepted in Proc. IEEE/RSJ IROS
summary: 3D scene graphs provide a hierarchical abstraction of environments by encoding spatial entities, such as objects and places, and their relationships. However, existing scene graph systems model object geometry coarsely, relying on partial point clouds or class-level CAD templates, which limits instance-specific shape detail. This paper presents Hydra++, a system-level investigation into how learning-based object shape estimators can be integrated into a hierarchical 3D scene graph pipeline. Hydra++ incorporates category-agnostic shape estimation and a reprojection-mask consistency check to reject degenerate predictions from partial observations or imprecise segmentation. In its default CRISP-based configuration, Hydra++ performs online scene graph construction; slower estimators such as SAM3D are evaluated as modular alternatives to demonstrate generalization-latency trade-offs. Furthermore, to address the challenges of sparse and noisy depth measurements in outdoor environments, Hydra++ supports a hybrid LiDAR-camera configuration for large-scale operation, improving scene-level reconstruction quality. Experiments in both simulation and real-world outdoor campus scenarios demonstrate that Hydra++ improves object- and scene-level reconstruction quality. Project page is available at https://hydra-plusplus.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Hydra++ integrates learning-based shape estimators into hierarchical 3D scene graphs, using category-agnostic shape estimation and reprojection-mask consistency checks, with hybrid LiDAR-camera support for outdoor environments, improving object- and scene-level reconstruction quality.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D scene graph systems model object geometry coarsely using partial point clouds or class-level CAD templates, lacking instance-specific shape detail.
AI.method: Hydra++ integrates category-agnostic shape estimation and a reprojection-mask consistency check to reject degenerate predictions; uses CRISP-based configuration for online construction with SAM3D as modular alternative; supports hybrid LiDAR-camera configuration for outdoor large-scale operation.
AI.result: Hydra++ improves object- and scene-level reconstruction quality in both simulation and real-world outdoor campus scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Learning-based object shape estimators can be effectively integrated into hierarchical 3D scene graphs to enhance geometric detail, with trade-offs between generalization and latency, and hybrid sensor configurations enable robust outdoor operation.

title: Super-Tuning: From Activation-Aware Pruning to Sparse Fine-Tuning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) remain expensive to fine-tune because full-parameter updates require substantial memory, compute, and per-task storage. We study whether saliency signals originally developed for pruning can be reused to choose where a model should adapt. We propose Super, a sparse parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method that fixes a small trainable support using a Wanda-style activation-weighted magnitude score [Sun et al., 2023] computed from a calibration pass. We then introduce Supra, a hybrid adapter that combines this sparse update with LoRA while preserving a matched trainable-parameter budget through a simple budget-splitting rule. In single-seed Math17K arithmetic experiments on Llama-3.2-1B and Meta-Llama-3-8B, the best Super/Supra variants achieve the highest average accuracy among the tested schedule-selected adapter configurations. We also include a PaFi-style magnitude-only support as a closest training-free sparse baseline and find that low-score supports under both magnitude and Wanda-style orderings can be effective. These results suggest that simple pruning-inspired orderings can provide useful fixed sparse supports for PEFT, especially when combined with low-rank adapters.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Super (sparse PEFT using Wanda-style saliency scores) and Supra (hybrid sparse+LoRA adapter with budget splitting), showing on Llama-3.2-1B and Llama-3-8B arithmetic tasks that pruning-inspired saliency signals can effectively determine fixed sparse supports for parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Full-parameter fine-tuning of LLMs is expensive in memory, compute, and per-task storage. The authors investigate whether saliency signals originally designed for pruning can be repurposed to select where a model should adapt, enabling more efficient fine-tuning.
AI.method: Super uses a Wanda-style activation-weighted magnitude score computed from a calibration pass to fix a small trainable support. Supra is a hybrid adapter combining this sparse update with LoRA using a budget-splitting rule to maintain a matched parameter budget.
AI.result: On Math17K arithmetic experiments with Llama-3.2-1B and Meta-Llama-3-8B, Super/Supra variants achieved the highest average accuracy among tested schedule-selected adapter configurations. Low-score supports under both magnitude and Wanda-style orderings can be effective.
AI.conclusion: Simple pruning-inspired orderings can provide useful fixed sparse supports for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, especially when combined with low-rank adapters like LoRA.

title: Foveation-Guided Dynamic Token Selection for Robust and Efficient Vision Transformers
summary: The human visual system (HVS) employs foveated sampling and eye movements to achieve efficient perception, conserving both metabolic energy and computational resources. Drawing inspiration from this robustness and adaptability, we introduce the Foveated Dynamic Transformer (FDT), a foveation-guided dynamic token-selection architecture that integrates these mechanisms into a vision transformer framework. The FDT exhibits strong resilience to various types of noise and adversarial attacks, despite not being explicitly trained for such challenges. This inherent robustness is achieved through the use of fixation and foveation modules: the fixation module identifies fixation points to filter out irrelevant information, while the foveation module generates foveated embeddings with multi-scale information. At the 50% fixation-budget setting, FDT achieves higher accuracy than DeiT-S (81.9% vs. 80.9%) while reducing multiply-accumulate operations by 34.57%, highlighting one operating point on its accuracy-efficiency trade-off. These attributes position FDT as an HVS-inspired step toward artificial neural networks that combine adaptive computation with improved resilience.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FDT, a vision transformer that mimics human foveated vision and eye movements to dynamically select tokens, achieving improved robustness to noise/adversarial attacks and better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs (e.g., 81.9% accuracy vs DeiT-S 80.9% with 34.57% fewer MACs at 50% fixation budget).
AI.motivation: To create vision transformers that are more efficient and robust by emulating the human visual system's foveated sampling and eye movement strategies, which naturally conserve energy and computational resources while maintaining perceptual resilience.
AI.method: FDT integrates foveation-guided dynamic token selection into a vision transformer using two key modules: (1) a fixation module that identifies fixation points to filter out irrelevant information, and (2) a foveation module that generates foveated embeddings with multi-scale information.
AI.result: At 50% fixation-budget, FDT achieves 81.9% accuracy (vs DeiT-S 80.9%) while reducing MAC operations by 34.57%, demonstrating both improved accuracy and efficiency. The model also exhibits inherent robustness to various noise types and adversarial attacks without explicit adversarial training.
AI.conclusion: FDT is a promising HVS-inspired step toward ANNs that combine adaptive computation with improved resilience, validating that bio-inspired foveation mechanisms can enhance both efficiency and robustness in vision transformers.

title: Risk-Aware General-Utility Markov Decision Processes
summary: We study general-utility Markov decision processes (GUMDPs) with risk-aware objectives. In this framework, an agent aims to optimize a risk measure of the distribution of objective values, where the objective function depends on the frequency of visitation of states induced by the agent's policy. First, we motivate, propose, and formalize risk-aware GUMDPs, which enable agents and decision makers to trade off expected performance by risk aversion while benefiting from the rich set of objectives that can be cast under the framework of GUMDPs. We focus our attention on the entropic risk measure (ERM). Second, we show how we can solve risk-aware GUMDPs with ERM objectives by resorting to online planning techniques. In particular, we propose an approach based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to provably solve risk-aware GUMDPs up to any desired accuracy. Third, we provide a set of experimental results showcasing that our approach is successful when optimizing for a spectrum of risk-aware behaviors in the context of GUMDPs under diverse tasks (standard MDPs, maximum state entropy exploration, imitation learning, and multi-objective MDPs).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces risk-aware general-utility Markov decision processes (GUMDPs) with entropic risk measures, proposes an MCTS-based online planning algorithm to solve them provably up to arbitrary accuracy, and demonstrates successful risk-aware behavior optimization across diverse tasks including standard MDPs, maximum entropy exploration, imitation learning, and multi-objective MDPs.
AI.motivation: To extend the GUMDP framework to incorporate risk-aware objectives, enabling agents to trade off expected performance with risk aversion while leveraging the rich class of objectives GUMDPs support.
AI.method: Formalizes risk-aware GUMDPs with entropic risk measure (ERM) objectives; develops an online planning algorithm based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) that provably solves these problems up to any desired accuracy.
AI.result: Experimental results show the proposed MCTS approach successfully optimizes risk-aware behaviors across diverse tasks: standard MDPs, maximum state entropy exploration, imitation learning, and multi-objective MDPs.
AI.conclusion: Risk-aware GUMDPs with ERM can be effectively solved via MCTS-based online planning, offering a flexible framework for trading off risk and reward across a wide range of sequential decision-making problems.

title: Decoupling Language Guidance from Backbones for Text-Guided Medical Segmentation
summary: Text-guided medical image segmentation leverages clinical semantics to improve lesion delineation, yet many existing models bind cross-modal fusion, supervision, and decoder design into a task-specific architecture. Such tight coupling makes it difficult to reuse language guidance modules across heterogeneous vision and text backbones, and often requires redesigning the network when the encoder pair changes. This paper presents BTHA, a backbone-transferable hierarchical adapter framework for text-guided medical image segmentation. BTHA is built around a stable feature-level interface: given multi-scale visual features and a text representation, it injects semantic guidance through shape-preserving adapters while maintaining the decoder-side tensor contract. To make this interface effective, we introduce a Hierarchical Coarse-to-Fine Supervision Strategy that decomposes learning into global image-text alignment, multi-scale auxiliary localization, and boundary-aware final mask refinement. We further design a Scale-Adaptive Gated Semantic Guidance (SAGSG) adapter, where resolution-specific gates adaptively control textual injection and channel recalibration suppresses redundant cross-modal responses. Evaluations across diverse vision and text backbones show that the same adapter and supervision design remains effective across convolutional and transformer-based visual encoders as well as different language encoders. Experiments on four public datasets further demonstrate that BTHA improves strong text-guided baselines with modest computational overhead.

AI.tldr: BTHA is a backbone-transferable hierarchical adapter framework for text-guided medical image segmentation that decouples cross-modal fusion from task-specific architectures via shape-preserving adapters and a hierarchical supervision strategy, achieving consistent improvement across diverse vision and text backbones on four public datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing text-guided medical image segmentation models tightly couple cross-modal fusion, supervision, and decoder design into task-specific architectures, making it difficult to reuse language guidance modules across heterogeneous vision and text backbones and requiring network redesign when encoder pairs change.
AI.method: BTHA introduces three key components: (1) a stable feature-level interface using shape-preserving adapters that inject semantic guidance while maintaining decoder tensor contracts; (2) a Hierarchical Coarse-to-Fine Supervision Strategy with global image-text alignment, multi-scale auxiliary localization, and boundary-aware final mask refinement; (3) a Scale-Adaptive Gated Semantic Guidance (SAGSG) adapter with resolution-specific gates for adaptive textual injection and channel recalibration to suppress redundant cross-modal responses.
AI.result: The same adapter and supervision design remains effective across convolutional and transformer-based visual encoders as well as different language encoders. Evaluations on four public datasets show that BTHA improves strong text-guided baselines with modest computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: BTHA demonstrates that decoupling cross-modal fusion from specific backbone architectures via a backbone-transferable adapter framework is an effective and efficient approach for text-guided medical image segmentation, enabling seamless reuse across diverse encoder combinations.

title: Shortcut Trajectory Planning for Efficient Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Diffusion-based trajectory planners have shown strong performance in offline reinforcement learning, but their iterative denoising process often incurs high inference cost. Consistency-based planners reduce the number of sampling steps, yet they typically rely on a two-stage teacher--student distillation pipeline that increases training cost and may introduce instability. We propose Shortcut Trajectory Planning (STP), an offline model-based reinforcement learning framework that incorporates shortcut models as efficient trajectory generators. STP trains a conditional shortcut trajectory model in a single stage, supports adjustable one-step and few-step inference through step-size conditioning, and selects candidate plans using a critic augmented with feasibility-aware correction. Across standard D4RL benchmarks, including locomotion, navigation, manipulation, and dexterous control tasks, STP achieves strong performance while simplifying the training pipeline for fast generative planning.

AI.tldr: STP is a single-stage, adjustable-step trajectory planner that uses shortcut models for efficient offline RL, achieving strong performance with simplified training and fast inference.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based planners suffer from high inference cost due to iterative denoising, while consistency-based planners reduce inference steps but require costly two-stage teacher-student distillation that introduces training instability.
AI.method: STP trains a conditional shortcut trajectory model in a single stage with step-size conditioning for adjustable one-step/few-step inference, and selects candidate plans using a critic with feasibility-aware correction.
AI.result: Achieves strong performance across D4RL benchmarks (locomotion, navigation, manipulation, dexterous control) while simplifying the training pipeline.
AI.conclusion: STP provides efficient generative planning with a streamlined single-stage training approach, matching or exceeding the performance of diffusion-based and consistency-based planners at lower computational cost.

title: SigLIP-HD by Fine-to-Coarse Supervision
summary: High-quality visual representation is a long-standing pursuit in computer vision. In the context of multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), feeding higher-resolution images can produce more fine-grained visual tokens. However, it introduces additional computational and design complexity, due to multiple forward passes and post-processing of increased tokens. Before simply adopting a higher resolution, have we truly unlocked the model's full perception capability at a standard resolution? Therefore, we study an interesting problem: how to achieve fine visual perception under lower cost without larger images. We present SigLIP-HD in this work. The core is a highly simple fine-to-coarse supervision design. We enforce the coarse feature of a mid-resolution image to mimic the fine-grained feature of its high-resolution version. We build this framework on the advanced SigLIP 2 model. Our final model produces better visual tokens at exactly the same inference budget. It is validated on extensive MLLM benchmarks and consistently delivers stronger results than our baseline model, especially on OCR-related tasks.

AI.tldr: SigLIP-HD improves visual perception in MLLMs by training mid-resolution features to mimic high-resolution features, achieving better performance at standard resolution without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: To achieve fine-grained visual perception under lower computational cost without actually using larger images, questioning whether models' full perception capability at standard resolution has been properly unlocked.
AI.method: A simple fine-to-coarse supervision design where coarse features from mid-resolution images are trained to mimic fine-grained features from their high-resolution counterparts, built on the SigLIP 2 model.
AI.result: Better visual tokens at the same inference budget, with consistent improvements across MLLM benchmarks, especially on OCR-related tasks.
AI.conclusion: Fine visual perception can be achieved at standard resolution without scaling to larger images, effectively reducing computational and design complexity while improving performance.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Scalable and Transferable Node Centrality Approximation
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) provide a learning-based framework for approximating graph quantities that are expensive to compute exactly. This paper investigates GNNs for scalable approximation of betweenness and closeness centrality, formulated as a node-ranking problem. Exact centrality values are used as supervision, and ranking quality is evaluated using Kendall's tau rank correlation. We study whether message-passing GNNs can learn transferable structural representations across different graph topologies rather than only fitting the distribution used during training. On unseen Erdos renyi graphs, the proposed models achieve tau = 0.851 for betweenness and tau = 0.894 for closeness. A large-scale betweenness model trained on graphs with N = 5,000 nodes achieves tau = 0.938, demonstrating scalability. Mixed-distribution training on Erdos renyi, Barabasi-Albert, and Gaussian Random Partition graphs improves betweenness transfer across graph families. In contrast, closeness centrality remains more sensitive to community-structured graphs and shows reduced transfer to real-world topologies. Finally, GNN inference achieves up to a 97.7x speedup over exact computation. These results show that mixed-distribution training can improve structural transfer in GNN-based centrality approximation, while identifying closeness centrality's sensitivity to topology as an open challenge.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates GNNs for scalable approximation of betweenness and closeness centrality, showing strong transfer across graph topologies with mixed-distribution training, achieving high Kendall's tau correlation and up to 97.7x speedup over exact computation.
AI.motivation: Centrality metrics like betweenness and closeness are computationally expensive to compute exactly on large graphs. The authors aim to develop GNN-based approximations that are scalable and can transfer across different graph topologies.
AI.method: Message-passing GNNs are trained with exact centrality values as supervision on synthetic graphs (Erdos-Renyi, Barabasi-Albert, Gaussian Random Partition). The model is evaluated using Kendall's tau rank correlation on unseen graphs from different distributions and real-world topologies. Mixed-distribution training is employed to improve transferability.
AI.result: On unseen Erdos-Renyi graphs, tau=0.851 for betweenness and tau=0.894 for closeness. A large-scale model (N=5,000) achieves tau=0.938 for betweenness. Mixed-distribution training improves betweenness transfer across graph families. GNN inference achieves up to 97.7x speedup over exact computation.
AI.conclusion: Mixed-distribution training enhances structural transfer for GNN-based centrality approximation, but closeness centrality remains sensitive to community-structured graphs and shows reduced transfer to real-world topologies, posing an open challenge.

title: What VGGT Knows About Overlap: Probing Geometric Foundation Models for Co-Visibility
summary: A fundamental challenge in 3D reconstruction and robotic localization is co-visibility: determining which image pairs share overlapping visible surfaces, particularly in scenarios with minimal overlap. We demonstrate that VGGT implicitly encodes co-visibility as an emergent behavior: without any supervision for this task, its internal representations exhibit a clear hierarchical structure mirroring that of large language models, i.e. early layers build a 3D-aware scene representation, while late layers act as dedicated co-visibility reasoners. In particular, we identify layer L17 as a negative anchor that consistently routes non-co-visible pairs for this backbone, regardless of the evaluation setting, providing task-grounded evidence of layer specialization in a geometry-grounded foundation model. Building on this, we introduce Co-VGGT, which freezes VGGT and trains only a lightweight layer-wise mixture-of-experts head (less than 7.5M parameters) to classify co-visibility from RGB alone, treating each layer as a specialized expert whose geometric abstraction is adaptively weighted per input pair. On the Co-VisiON benchmark, Co-VGGT surpasses the human annotation baseline and improves over prior work by more than 25% pairwise and 10% multiview. Pairwise predictions are well-calibrated (ECE=0.030), enabling direct use as edge weights in visibility graphs for downstream SfM and SLAM pipelines without post-hoc correction. Code and data are available.

AI.tldr: VGGT implicitly encodes co-visibility as an emergent behavior without supervision. Co-VGGT freezes VGGT and trains a lightweight MoE head (<7.5M params) to classify co-visibility from RGB, surpassing human baselines by 25% pairwise and 10% multiview on Co-VisiON benchmark.
AI.motivation: Co-visibility (determining which image pairs share overlapping visible surfaces) is a fundamental challenge in 3D reconstruction and robotic localization, especially in scenarios with minimal overlap.
AI.method: Identify that VGGT's internal representations exhibit hierarchical structure: early layers build 3D-aware scene representation, late layers act as co-visibility reasoners. Layer L17 is a negative anchor for non-co-visible pairs. Co-VGGT freezes VGGT and trains a lightweight layer-wise mixture-of-experts head (<7.5M parameters) that adaptively weights each layer's geometric abstraction per input pair to classify co-visibility from RGB alone.
AI.result: Surpasses human annotation baseline and improves over prior work by >25% pairwise and 10% multiview on Co-VisiON benchmark. Pairwise predictions are well-calibrated (ECE=0.030), enabling direct use as edge weights in visibility graphs for downstream SfM and SLAM.
AI.conclusion: VGGT exhibits emergent co-visibility reasoning without supervision, and Co-VGGT provides a lightweight, calibrated solution that can be directly integrated into downstream 3D pipelines.

title: Mach-Mind-4-Flash Technical Report
summary: We present Mach-Mind-4-Flash, a 35B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic model with 3B activated parameters. Through post-training optimization alone without scaling pre-training compute, the model achieves performance on par with or surpassing that of 100B-parameter-class models. By introducing scalable agentic interaction environments for large-scale reinforcement learning, the model attains significant performance gains on real-world application tasks. Our pipeline comprises three stages: (1) a unified RL/OPD training infrastructure with dynamic multi-teacher scheduling and operator-level acceleration, delivering 17\% end-to-end training speedup; (2) multiple domain-specific RL experts trained in parallel across Reasoning, General, and Agent tracks, then fused into a single generalist via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) -- a routed reverse-KL objective that eliminates the see-saw degradation of mixed-reward RL; (3) Hybrid Median-length Policy Optimization (HMPO), a single-stage token-efficiency method that compresses reasoning chains by 19--46\% with $\le$0.7 percentage-point accuracy loss. Mach-Mind-4-Flash scores 92.70 on AIME'26, 82.82 on IFBench, 80.74 on Behavioral-SafetyBench, 75.80 on BFCL-v4, 72.31 on BrowseComp-zh, and 84.20 on ClawBench -- leading or matching models with 10--30$\times$ its activated size at a fraction of the inference cost.

AI.tldr: Mach-Mind-4-Flash is a 35B MoE model (3B active params) that, via post-training optimization alone, matches or surpasses 100B-class models. It uses a three-stage pipeline: (1) unified RL/OPD infrastructure with 17% speedup; (2) Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to fuse domain-specific experts without see-saw degradation; (3) Hybrid Median-length Policy Optimization (HMPO) compressing reasoning chains by 19-46% with ≤0.7% accuracy loss. Achieves leading scores on multiple benchmarks at fraction of inference cost.
AI.motivation: To achieve high performance with extremely efficient inference (3B activated parameters) without scaling pre-training compute, leveraging only post-training optimization including large-scale RL in agentic environments.
AI.method: Three-stage post-training pipeline: (1) unified RL/OPD infrastructure with dynamic multi-teacher scheduling and operator-level acceleration; (2) Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) with routed reverse-KL objective to fuse parallel-trained domain experts (Reasoning, General, Agent) into a single generalist; (3) Hybrid Median-length Policy Optimization (HMPO) for single-stage token-efficiency compression.
AI.result: AIME'26: 92.70, IFBench: 82.82, Behavioral-SafetyBench: 80.74, BFCL-v4: 75.80, BrowseComp-zh: 72.31, ClawBench: 84.20. Outperforms or matches models 10-30× its activated size.
AI.conclusion: Post-training optimization alone can bridge the gap between small activated-parameter models and much larger models, achieving competitive or superior performance with dramatically lower inference cost.

title: DGSfM: Depth-Guided Scale-Aware Global Structure-from-Motion
summary: Global Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is an efficient paradigm for recovering camera poses and sparse 3D structure from unordered images. However, its reliance on scale-ambiguous epipolar geometry makes global positioning sensitive to noisy baseline estimates and weak view-graph constraints, while false edges from visually ambiguous pairs can further degrade reconstruction. We propose DGSfM, a depth-aware global SfM pipeline that uses monocular depth maps as a scalable prior while preserving explicit multi-view optimization. For each image pair, we use a depth-aware relative pose solver to convert scale-ambiguous epipolar constraints into scale-aware relative pose constraints. We further improve robustness through view-graph filtering and depth-consistency-based correspondence pruning, which suppress false edges and matches that remain plausible under epipolar geometry alone. Finally, global scale averaging and depth-guided pose-point initialization align monocular depth maps into a common reconstruction scale and provide stable initialization for global positioning and bundle adjustment. Experiments on ETH3D and IMC2021 show that DGSfM consistently improves over strong global SfM baselines across sparse and dense matching front-ends, achieving substantial gains in pose accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/sithu31296/DGSfM.

AI.tldr: DGSfM is a depth-aware global Structure-from-Motion pipeline that leverages monocular depth maps as a scalable prior to resolve scale ambiguity, improves robustness via view-graph filtering and depth-consistency pruning, and achieves substantial pose accuracy gains on ETH3D and IMC2021 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Global SfM relies on scale-ambiguous epipolar geometry, making it sensitive to noisy baseline estimates, weak view-graph constraints, and false edges from visually ambiguous pairs, which degrade reconstruction quality.
AI.method: (1) Depth-aware relative pose solver converting scale-ambiguous epipolar constraints into scale-aware relative pose constraints; (2) View-graph filtering and depth-consistency-based correspondence pruning to suppress false edges and matches; (3) Global scale averaging and depth-guided pose-point initialization to align monocular depth maps into a common reconstruction scale and provide stable initialization for global positioning and bundle adjustment.
AI.result: Consistent improvement over strong global SfM baselines across sparse and dense matching front-ends on ETH3D and IMC2021 datasets, with substantial gains in pose accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Monocular depth maps serve as an effective scalable prior for global SfM, resolving scale ambiguity and improving robustness without sacrificing explicit multi-view optimization.

title: Learning Physics-Informed Surrogate Model of Linear Elastic Displacement Fields from Geometry
summary: This work aims to develop a fast and physically consistent surrogate model for real-time structural health monitoring of fractured elastic domains. We propose a physics-informed DeepONet framework that predicts displacement fields from both boundary conditions and fracture geometry, using a dedicated encoding strategy for the latter and without relying on finite-element-generated training data. The traction-free condition on the fracture boundary is imposed weakly through a localized penalty term. The presented numerical example focuses on one representative fracture geometry, demonstrating the feasibility of the formulation and laying the groundwork for extensions to surrogate modeling across diverse fracture geometries.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a physics-informed DeepONet surrogate model for real-time structural health monitoring of fractured elastic domains. It predicts displacement fields from boundary conditions and fracture geometry using a dedicated encoding strategy and a localized penalty term for traction-free conditions, without relying on finite-element training data. A numerical example demonstrates feasibility for one fracture geometry.
AI.motivation: To develop a fast, physically consistent surrogate model for real-time structural health monitoring of fractured elastic domains that does not rely on finite-element-generated training data.
AI.method: A physics-informed DeepONet framework that encodes fracture geometry with a dedicated strategy, imposes traction-free conditions weakly via a localized penalty term, and predicts displacement fields from both boundary conditions and fracture geometry without FE-generated data.
AI.result: Numerical example on one representative fracture geometry demonstrates feasibility of the formulation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach is feasible for surrogate modeling of fractured elastic domains, laying groundwork for extension to diverse fracture geometries.

title: Seeing is Free, Speaking is Not: Uncovering the True Energy Bottleneck in Edge VLM Inference
comment: Accepted to ACM MM 2026. 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are the perceptual backbone of embodied AI, but their energy footprint on edge hardware remains poorly understood. Existing efficiency efforts focus predominantly on reducing visual tokens, implicitly treating visual processing as the dominant energy cost. We overturn this implicit assumption through the first systematic energy profiling of on-device VLM inference, spanning five models across three architecture families, four input resolutions, and two hardware platforms (NVIDIA RTX 3070 and Jetson Orin NX). Our analysis yields three findings. First, average inference power is a model-intrinsic constant, invariant to input resolution, image complexity, and prompt type, with less than 5% variation across all conditions. This means that all energy variation across inputs must arise from variation in inference time, not from variation in power draw. Second, each output token costs 11 to 39x more wall-clock time than each input token due to the compute-bound and memory-bound asymmetry between prefill and decode, making output token count the dominant driver of both latency and energy. Third, image complexity, measured by the number of objects in an image, induces up to 4.1x energy differences at identical resolution. This variation arises not from increased visual processing cost, but from differences in output length. These findings expose a fundamental limitation of visual token pruning: even removing all visual tokens saves at most 10% of total energy for fixed-token models. Across models spanning 1 billion to 8 billion parameters, controlling output length saves up to 97% of total energy, with the energy dominance of decoding growing stronger at larger model scale. In short, the true energy bottleneck in edge VLM inference is not what the model sees, but how much it says.

AI.tldr: This paper overturns the assumption that visual processing dominates energy consumption in on-device VLM inference. Through systematic profiling, the authors find that output token count is the dominant driver of both latency and energy—each output token costs 11-39x more time than input tokens. Visual token pruning saves at most 10% of total energy, while controlling output length can save up to 97% of total energy. The energy bottleneck is not what the model sees, but how much it says.
AI.motivation: To understand the true energy consumption patterns of VLM inference on edge hardware, challenging the prevailing assumption that visual token reduction is the most effective efficiency strategy.
AI.method: Systematic energy profiling of on-device VLM inference across five models, three architecture families, four input resolutions, and two hardware platforms (NVIDIA RTX 3070 and Jetson Orin NX), measuring power draw, latency, and energy under varying input and output conditions.
AI.result: (1) Average inference power is a model-intrinsic constant (<5% variation). (2) Each output token costs 11-39x more time than each input token, making output count the dominant energy driver. (3) Image complexity induces up to 4.1x energy differences via output length variation. Visual token pruning saves at most 10% energy; controlling output length saves up to 97%.
AI.conclusion: The true energy bottleneck in edge VLM inference is decoding (output token generation), not visual processing. Future efficiency efforts should prioritize controlling output length rather than reducing visual tokens.

title: Fully Trainable Deep Differentiable Logic Gate Networks and Lookup Table Networks
summary: We introduce a novel method for both partial and full optimization of the connections in deep differentiable logic gate networks (LGNs) and lookup table networks (LUTNs). Our training method utilizes a probability distribution over a set of connections per gate/lookup table (LUT) input pin, selecting the connection with highest merit, all whilst the optimal gate types or LUT-entries are learned in parallel. We show that the connection-optimized LGNs outperform standard fixed-connection LGNs on the Yin-Yang, MNIST Handwritten Digits and Fashion-MNIST benchmarks, while requiring only a fraction of the number of logic gates. We achieve 98.92% on the MNIST dataset with two layers of 8000 gates. With only one layer of 8000 gates, we obtain 98.45%, showing that our method requires almost 50 times fewer gates compared to fixed-connection LGNs. Training stability up to ten layers has been ensured by employing a high learning rate, straight-through estimators and trimming constant-output gate types. Additionally, we present a LUT neuron description that enables stable training with backpropagation, tested up to 6-layer deep networks. The model requires four times fewer trainable parameters and still achieves a higher accuracy compared to the fixed-connection LGN training algorithm. Our connection-training algorithm also works well for the LUTNs, achieving an accuracy of 98.88% for two layers of 2000 6-input LUTs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a connection optimization method for logic gate networks (LGNs) and lookup table networks (LUTNs) that uses probabilistic connection selection per input pin, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with significantly fewer gates and parameters compared to fixed-connection baselines.
AI.motivation: To improve the efficiency and performance of deep differentiable logic gate networks and lookup table networks by optimizing not just the gate/LUT types but also the connections between them, reducing the number of required logic gates while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.method: A training method that maintains a probability distribution over a set of candidate connections per gate/LUT input pin, selecting the highest-merit connection during training, while simultaneously learning optimal gate types or LUT entries via backpropagation with straight-through estimators and high learning rates.
AI.result: 98.92% on MNIST with two layers of 8000 gates (98.45% with one layer), nearly 50× fewer gates than fixed-connection LGNs; 98.88% on MNIST with two layers of 2000 6-input LUTs; models use four times fewer trainable parameters while achieving higher accuracy than fixed-connection baselines.
AI.conclusion: Connection optimization is an effective strategy for drastically reducing the model size of LGNs and LUTNs without sacrificing accuracy, and the method scales stably up to at least 10 layers for LGNs and 6 layers for LUTNs.

title: ALICE: Learning a General-Purpose Pathology Foundation Model from Vision, Vision-Language, and Slide-Level Experts
summary: Foundation models are reshaping computational pathology, yet their capabilities remain shaped by pretraining objectives, data sources, and spatial scales, fragmenting complementary expertise across separate backbones. Here we present ALICE, a unified foundation model trained through multi-stage agglomerative distillation that sequentially distills eight vision-only, vision-language, and slide-level teacher models into dedicated modules of a single backbone. ALICE is pretrained on 24,985,184 tile-level pathology images and 155,604 high-resolution images, and evaluated across 21 task scenarios, 96 downstream tasks, and 48 data sources, spanning region-of-interest tissue analysis, vision-language multimodal evaluation, and whole-slide clinical assessment. In all three evaluation settings, ALICE achieved the best average rank among task-matched pathology foundation models. These results demonstrate that agglomerative distillation can consolidate complementary capabilities from specialized models into a unified backbone for broad computational pathology applications. The model is available at https://github.com/WonderLandxD/ALICE.

AI.tldr: ALICE is a unified pathology foundation model trained via multi-stage agglomerative distillation from eight specialist teacher models (vision-only, vision-language, and slide-level) into a single backbone, pretrained on ~25M tile-level and ~155K high-resolution images, achieving the best average rank across 96 downstream tasks spanning tissue analysis, multimodal evaluation, and whole-slide clinical assessment.
AI.motivation: Existing pathology foundation models are fragmented across different pretraining objectives, data sources, and spatial scales, requiring separate backbones with complementary but non-unified capabilities.
AI.method: Multi-stage agglomerative distillation: sequentially distills knowledge from eight teacher models (vision-only, vision-language, and slide-level) into dedicated modules of a single backbone. Pretrained on 24,985,184 tile-level and 155,604 high-resolution pathology images.
AI.result: Evaluated across 21 task scenarios, 96 downstream tasks, and 48 data sources. Achieved the best average rank among task-matched pathology foundation models across three evaluation settings: region-of-interest tissue analysis, vision-language multimodal evaluation, and whole-slide clinical assessment.
AI.conclusion: Agglomerative distillation can consolidate complementary capabilities from specialized models into a unified backbone for broad computational pathology applications.

title: On-Device Adaptive Battery Power Prediction for Electric Vehicles
comment: 6 pages, 3 tables, 5 figures; Accepted to IEEE EdgeCom 2025
summary: Adaptive power management in Electric Vehicles (EVs) requires accurate power prediction. Although deep learning models have emerged as highly effective for time-series forecasting in this domain, their performance is prone to degradation when exposed to data with distributions different from the training data. We introduce a novel approach that enables on-device learning in resource-constrained EV systems to continuously adapt pretrained battery prediction models to new, unseen data. We leverage existing pretrained models by transforming them into adaptable versions that retain critical hyperparameter knowledge from their initial training. We comprehensively investigate both online and offline model adaptation strategies. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in forecasting performance across various models and time horizons, achieving mean absolute error reductions of up to 7.49\% and 14.88\% with online and offline adaptation techniques, respectively. This study highlights the substantial benefit of on-device adaptation, resulting in enhanced battery power predictions than unadapted model deployments in real-world EV scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces on-device learning approaches for adapting pretrained battery prediction models to new data in resource-constrained EV systems, achieving significant error reductions through online (up to 7.49%) and offline (up to 14.88%) adaptation strategies.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for EV battery power prediction suffer performance degradation when exposed to data distributions different from training data, necessitating adaptive on-device learning solutions for resource-constrained systems.
AI.method: The authors transform pretrained models into adaptable versions preserving critical hyperparameter knowledge, and comprehensively investigate both online and offline model adaptation strategies for on-device learning.
AI.result: Achieved mean absolute error reductions of up to 7.49% with online adaptation and 14.88% with offline adaptation across various models and time horizons.
AI.conclusion: On-device adaptation substantially enhances battery power predictions compared to unadapted model deployments in real-world EV scenarios.

title: The Count Is There, but Misaligned: Understanding and Correcting Counting Failures in VLMs
summary: Despite strong performance on many multimodal tasks, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with basic object counting. We investigate whether this reflects missing internal knowledge or a gap between internal representations and verbalized outputs. Training simple probes on activations from four VLMs across five counting datasets reveals that nonlinear probes can reliably detect counting errors, suggesting that VLMs often encode the correct count even when they output the wrong answer. SVCCA analysis shows that probes trained on ground-truth counts and probes trained on model outputs occupy a partially shared activation subspace but read out along misaligned directions. We further validate our findings using a causal steering intervention, proving that strengthening the direction of count-identified probes does improve model counting performance. Motivated by this result, we propose a detector-guided self-correction method that selectively re-prompts the model only when an internal error detector predicts failure. This simple inference-time intervention improves counting accuracy by up to 15.6 absolute percentage points, without any parameter updates. Our results establish activation-based error probing as both a practical tool for improving VLM counting and a mechanistic lens on the gap between internal knowledge and model outputs.

AI.tldr: VLMs often internally encode correct object counts even when outputting wrong answers; probing activations and steering interventions can detect and correct counting errors, improving accuracy by up to 15.6% without parameter updates.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether VLM counting failures stem from missing internal knowledge or a disconnect between internal representations and verbalized outputs, and to leverage this understanding for practical improvement.
AI.method: Trained linear/nonlinear probes on VLM activations (4 models, 5 datasets) to detect counting errors; used SVCCA to compare probe subspaces; applied causal steering intervention; proposed a detector-guided self-correction method that re-prompts the model only when internal errors are detected.
AI.result: Nonlinear probes reliably detect counting errors; probes trained on ground-truth vs. model outputs share a partial subspace but read out along misaligned directions; causal steering improves performance; detector-guided self-correction yields up to 15.6 absolute percentage point improvement in counting accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Activation-based error probing serves both as a practical inference-time tool for improving VLM counting and as a mechanistic lens to understand the gap between internal knowledge and model outputs.

title: Data-Efficient Deep Learning: Empirical Guidelines for Training Set Size Estimation in Inertial Sensor Classification
summary: Deep learning models dependency on large-scale inertial datasets presents a significant bottleneck in inertial sensor-based classification tasks, such as human activity recognition and smartphone location recognition. In these domains, data collection requires massive recording campaigns that are complex, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Currently, data-driven guidelines for determining the minimum sample size required to reach a desired accuracy level do not exist. To address this gap, this study presents a systematic empirical evaluation of learning curve convergence rates in inertial classification. We introduce a unified framework that analyzes classification performance under both binary and multi-class scenarios, and derive an empirical formula to estimate performance relative to dataset size. Testing across six diverse, real-world datasets totaling 102.7 hours of inertial measurements demonstrates that accuracy follows a consistent logarithmic growth pattern, regardless of task complexity. Leveraging this finding, we propose a quantitative stability point metric, defined as the sample size required for the learning curve to stabilize within a predefined mean absolute percentage deviation of its asymptotic maximum. Our analysis reveals that models often reach practical stability with substantially fewer samples than traditional heuristics suggest. Ultimately, we offer a generalizable framework to extrapolate total data requirements from small-scale pilot studies, optimizing the tradeoff between recording effort and model reliability. These findings shift the prevailing paradigm from maximizing data volume toward optimizing data efficiency, offering concrete, data-backed guidelines for planning recording campaigns in inertial sensing applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an empirical framework to determine minimum sample sizes needed for inertial sensor-based classification, showing that accuracy follows consistent logarithmic growth across datasets and introducing a stability point metric to optimize the tradeoff between data collection effort and model performance.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models require large-scale inertial datasets for tasks like activity and location recognition, but data collection is complex, time-consuming, and lacks guidelines for determining the minimum sample size needed to achieve a desired accuracy level.
AI.method: Systematic empirical evaluation of learning curve convergence rates across six diverse real-world datasets (totaling 102.7 hours); analysis of binary and multi-class scenarios; derivation of an empirical formula relating performance to dataset size; proposal of a stability point metric based on mean absolute percentage deviation from asymptotic maximum.
AI.result: Accuracy follows a consistent logarithmic growth pattern regardless of task complexity; models often reach practical stability with substantially fewer samples than traditional heuristics suggest.
AI.conclusion: Offers a generalizable framework to extrapolate total data requirements from small-scale pilot studies, shifting the paradigm from maximizing data volume toward optimizing data efficiency with concrete guidelines for planning recording campaigns.

title: TCLA: Training-Free Class-wise Logit Adaptation for Medical Vision-Language Models
summary: Medical Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot performance, yet their effectiveness still declines on out-of-distribution (OOD) data due to domain shifts and class bias inherited from large-scale pretraining. Existing few-shot adaptation methods typically introduce additional trainable components, which can be unstable in extremely low-data regimes (e.g., 1-shot), and lack robustness on different medical data. We present TCLA, a purely training-free few-shot adaptation method for Medical VLMs, which is fast and model-agnostic. TCLA corrects inference logits based on a small set of support samples, boosting pretrained VLMs performance by improving inter-class deconfusion and reducing domain shift. Extensive experiments on nine datasets across multiple medical imaging modalities including X-ray, Ultrasound, MRI, CT, Histopathology, demonstrate that TCLA consistently improves OOD performance of Medical VLMs and, in most of cases, outperforms existing training-based adaptation methods.

AI.tldr: TCLA is a training-free few-shot adaptation method for Medical VLMs that corrects inference logits using support samples to improve OOD performance across multiple imaging modalities, outperforming training-based methods in most cases.
AI.motivation: Medical VLMs suffer from performance decline on OOD data due to domain shifts and class bias from pretraining. Existing few-shot adaptation methods introduce trainable components that are unstable in extremely low-data regimes (e.g., 1-shot) and lack robustness across different medical data.
AI.method: TCLA is a purely training-free few-shot adaptation method that corrects inference logits based on a small set of support samples, improving inter-class deconfusion and reducing domain shift without adding trainable parameters.
AI.result: On nine datasets across X-ray, Ultrasound, MRI, CT, and Histopathology modalities, TCLA consistently improves OOD performance of Medical VLMs and outperforms existing training-based adaptation methods in most cases.
AI.conclusion: Training-free logit correction using support samples is an effective, fast, and model-agnostic approach for adapting Medical VLMs to OOD data, even outperforming training-based methods in low-data regimes.

title: SYNRARE: Synthetic Rare Disease EHR Generation for ML Benchmarking
comment: Intended for submission to the Application Notes Bioinformatics Journal
summary:
Motivation: Rare disease (RD) diagnosis is frequently delayed due to the similarities in symptoms to common disease variants. Machine Learning Algorithms applied to Electronic Health Records show promise for accelerating the diagnosis; however, legal and privacy concerns pose significant barriers. To address these issues, Synthetic Data Generation is an alternative method for obtaining Electronic Health Records and can be applied with any Machine Learning algorithm for benchmarking and development purposes. Despite the availability of Synthetic Data Generation algorithms, support for generating a subset of patients that differ in a definable degree from the majority to simulate patients with RD is often lacking.
  Results: We present SYNRARE, a graphical user interface based on the Synthea framework that enables easier modification and generation of synthetic Electronic Health Records of RD patients, which differ only to a definable degree from patients with common diseases, thereby enabling the benchmarking and testing of algorithms under controlled technical conditions. SYNRARE enables researchers to rapidly benchmark their Machine Learning algorithms across any scenario.
  Availability and implementation: SYNRARE, including detailed instructions for installing, is available at https://gitlab.sdu.dk/screen4care/synrare.

AI.tldr: SYNRARE is a graphical user interface built on the Synthea framework that generates synthetic Electronic Health Records for rare disease patients, allowing researchers to control the degree of difference from common disease patients to benchmark Machine Learning algorithms for rare disease diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Rare disease diagnosis is often delayed due to symptom similarity with common diseases. While ML algorithms on EHRs could help, legal and privacy barriers limit data access. Synthetic data generation offers a solution but lacks support for creating patient subsets that differ controllably from the majority to simulate rare diseases.
AI.method: SYNRARE is a GUI built on the Synthea framework that enables easier modification and generation of synthetic EHRs for rare disease patients, allowing users to define the degree of difference from common disease patients for controlled benchmarking.
AI.result: SYNRARE enables researchers to rapidly benchmark their ML algorithms across any scenario by generating synthetic rare disease patient records that differ to a definable degree from common disease patients.
AI.conclusion: SYNRARE addresses the lack of tools for generating controlled synthetic rare disease patient data, facilitating ML algorithm benchmarking and testing under controlled technical conditions while bypassing legal and privacy concerns.

title: Similarity search generalisation in contrastive learning with InfoNCE loss
summary: Similarity search is a primary application of embedding models trained by contrastive learning. For one of the most popular contrastive learning loss functions, InfoNCE, we show that the population risk with $k$ negative samples is $O(1/k)$ close to an expected cross-entropy which quantifies deviation between i) a softmax similarity search over unseen data using the learned embedding function, and ii) an idealised softmax search over the same data but using similarity implicitly represented in the positive sample generator. This complements existing interpretations of InfoNCE in the $k\to\infty$ limit which are phrased in terms of mutual information, and alignment versus uniformity in embeddings. To quantify generalisation performance, we introduce a new continuity bound for the InfoNCE loss, obtained via Gâteaux differentiation. The bound preserves the structure of averaging over negative samples present in the loss function and features an ``inverse temperature'' parameter which can be tuned to account for the algorithmic temperature. For embedding functions which are Lipschitz in a parameter, this yields a simple demonstration that the averaging effect of $k$ negative samples in the InfoNCE loss carries over to stabilisation of the generalisation error as $k$ grows.

AI.tldr: InfoNCE loss's population risk with k negatives is O(1/k) close to an expected cross-entropy measuring deviation between softmax similarity search on learned embeddings vs. an idealized search. A Gâteaux differentiation-based continuity bound shows the averaging effect of k negatives stabilizes generalization error.
AI.motivation: To theoretically understand and quantify the generalization performance of InfoNCE loss in contrastive learning for similarity search, beyond existing mutual information and alignment-uniformity interpretations.
AI.method: Analyzed population risk of InfoNCE with k negatives, deriving O(1/k) closeness to expected cross-entropy. Introduced Gâteaux differentiation to derive a continuity bound for InfoNCE loss that preserves negative sample averaging structure and incorporates an inverse temperature parameter.
AI.result: InfoNCE population risk converges to an expected cross-entropy at rate O(1/k). The Gâteaux-based continuity bound demonstrates that averaging over k negative samples stabilizes generalization error as k increases, for Lipschitz parameterized embedding functions.
AI.conclusion: Provides a new theoretical perspective on InfoNCE connecting it to softmax similarity search performance, and establishes that using more negative samples improves generalization stability via the averaging effect captured by the continuity bound.

title: Promptable Concept Segmentation from Above: Evaluating SAM 3's Zero-Shot and One-Shot Capabilities in Remote Sensing
summary: The deployment of large-scale foundation models, such as the Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3), promises a transition toward open-vocabulary, training-free computer vision. However, their capacity to generalize out-of-distribution to the complex, top-down geometric structures of Earth Observation imagery remains largely unquantified. Driven by SAM 3's performance disparities in highly specialized domains, we present a comprehensive, multi-task empirical evaluation across remote sensing scene classification, object detection, and instance segmentation under strict zero-shot and one-shot constraints. To achieve this, we introduce a structural adaptation of SAM 3 by repurposing its decoupled binary presence head into a standalone zero-shot classifier. Furthermore, by systematically isolating textual and visual prompt modalities across five configurations, we explicitly diagnose the alignment mechanics within the model's multimodal decoder. Our findings reveal severe cross-modal interference: while visual prompts successfully align the decoder to complex remote sensing geometry, textual prompts inject misaligned, ground-level semantic bias, actively degrading coordinate regression. To benchmark these capabilities without resource-intensive training, we formulate a novel training-free proxy evaluation protocol for Generalized Zero-Shot tasks (scene classification and instance segmentation). Ultimately, our results demonstrate that SAM 3 avoids the overfitting commonly seen in legacy domain-adapted models, achieving high Harmonic Mean scores in segmentation tasks. However, it remains fundamentally constrained by sub-pixel resolution limits and overhead semantic blind spots, charting a definitive mandate for parameter-efficient geospatial fine-tuning of its multimodal decoder.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates SAM 3's zero-shot and one-shot performance on remote sensing tasks (scene classification, object detection, instance segmentation). It introduces a structural adaptation using SAM 3's binary presence head as a zero-shot classifier, diagnoses cross-modal interference between visual and textual prompts, and proposes a training-free proxy evaluation protocol. Results show SAM 3 avoids overfitting but suffers from sub-pixel resolution limits and semantic blind spots, highlighting the need for parameter-efficient geospatial fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To quantify SAM 3's out-of-distribution generalization capacity for Earth Observation imagery, given its performance disparities in specialized domains, and to diagnose cross-modal alignment issues in its multimodal decoder under zero-shot/one-shot constraints.
AI.method: Multi-task empirical evaluation across scene classification, object detection, and instance segmentation under strict zero-shot and one-shot constraints; structural adaptation of SAM 3's decoupled binary presence head into a standalone zero-shot classifier; systematic isolation of textual and visual prompt modalities across five configurations to diagnose cross-modal interference; formulation of a training-free proxy evaluation protocol for Generalized Zero-Shot tasks.
AI.result: Visual prompts align the decoder to complex remote sensing geometry, but textual prompts inject misaligned ground-level semantic bias that degrades coordinate regression. SAM 3 avoids overfitting and achieves high Harmonic Mean scores in segmentation, but is constrained by sub-pixel resolution limits and overhead semantic blind spots.
AI.conclusion: SAM 3 demonstrates strong zero-shot segmentation capabilities without overfitting, but requires parameter-efficient geospatial fine-tuning of its multimodal decoder to address resolution and semantic limitations in Earth Observation tasks.
